chapters.title: Management: Concept, Principles, Roles and Skills
chapters.scope: What management is, how the classical writers said it should be done, and the roles and skills the job demands.

blocks.title: What management is
blocks.html:
Two chai stalls stand side by side with the same tea, the same prices and the same passing crowd. One makes money every month; the other runs out of milk by noon and loses its regulars. The difference is not the tea but how each owner runs the stall.

In plain wordsManagement is getting work done through other people, so that the goal is reached without wasting time, money or effort.

Exam definitionManagement is the process of designing and maintaining an environment in which individuals, working together in groups, efficiently accomplish selected aims (Koontz and Weihrich).

Two words carry the idea. Effectiveness is doing the right things, so the goal is met. Efficiency is doing things right, with the least waste of time, money and effort. Good management needs both.

An illustration. A college fest committee sells all 2,000 tickets it planned to sell, so it is effective. But it spends ₹6 lakh against a budget of ₹4 lakh, 50% over, so it is not efficient. A committee that saved money but sold only half the tickets would be efficient on paper and still fail its goal.

Writers have defined management in different words. Exams often ask who said which.

WriterManagement is…
Mary Parker Follettthe art of getting things done through people.
Harold Koontzthe art of getting things done through and with people in formally organised groups.
Koontz and Weihrichthe process of designing and maintaining an environment in which individuals, working together in groups, efficiently accomplish selected aims.
Peter Druckera multipurpose organ that manages a business, manages managers, and manages workers and work.
Dalton E. McFarlandthe process by which managers create, direct, maintain and operate purposive organisations through systematic, coordinated, cooperative human effort.

Nature. Management is:

  • goal-oriented, working toward set aims;
  • a continuous process, never finished;
  • universal: its principles apply to every kind of organisation, from a kirana store to a ministry;
  • a group activity, done through people;
  • intangible, seen only in its results;
  • multidisciplinary, drawing on economics, psychology, sociology and statistics;
  • both an art (skilled personal practice) and a science (a systematic body of knowledge).

It has many marks of a profession, such as a body of knowledge and formal training. Unlike medicine or law, though, entry to it is not restricted by a licence.

Levels. In a public-sector bank, the chairman and board sit at the top, zonal and regional heads in the middle, and the officers who supervise counter staff at a branch on the first line.

LevelWhoMain work
TopBoard of directors, chief executiveSets objectives, policy and strategy; answers to owners and society
MiddleHeads of departments and divisionsTurns policy into plans, coordinates departments, links top and bottom
First-line (lower)Supervisors, foremen, section officersDirects day-to-day work and reports results upward

Why it matters. Management reaches goals and uses resources with less waste. It coordinates departments and levels, avoids duplicated work, places competent people in each position, and prepares the organisation for a changing environment.

Don't confuse effectiveness with efficiency. Effectiveness asks whether the goal was reached; efficiency asks what it cost to reach it. Nor management with administration: some older writers, such as Oliver Sheldon, used administration for policy-making at the top and management for carrying it out. Others, such as E. F. L. Brech, treated management as the wider term, with administration as one part of it. Most modern textbooks treat the two words as one.

Where it breaks. "Universal" means the principles apply widely, not that a method can be copied unchanged. A practice that works in a Pune auto-parts plant may fail in a hospital or a cooperative. And management is an inexact science: its principles are guides that depend on people and circumstances, not laws like those of physics.

For exams. Match each definition to its writer. Know effective (right things) against efficient (things right), the features of management's nature, and the work of each level.

Right things (effective), done right (efficient), through people.

blocks.title: Fayol's 14 principles
blocks.html:
A new assistant at a bank branch gets one instruction from the branch manager and the opposite one from the operations head. She cannot obey both, and whichever she picks, someone is annoyed. A century ago Henri Fayol wrote a principle for exactly this.

In plain wordsFayol's principles are fourteen rules of thumb for arranging and running a whole organisation. They guide judgement; they are not fixed laws.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: principles of management are broad, general guidelines for managerial decisions and behaviour. Fayol set out fourteen of them in General and Industrial Management (1916).

Fayol was a French mining engineer who ran a large mining company. He wrote from the top of the organisation downward: his administrative principles describe how a whole enterprise should be arranged and run. He stressed that they are flexible, to be applied with a sense of proportion. They fall into four groups.

GroupPrinciples
Work and authority1 Division of work: specialise so that output and skill rise. 2 Authority and responsibility: the right to command comes with an equal duty to answer for results. 3 Discipline: respect for rules and agreements. 4 Unity of command: each employee takes orders from one superior.
Direction and organisational interest5 Unity of direction: one plan and one leader for activities with the same objective. 6 Subordination of individual interest to the general interest. 7 Remuneration: pay that is fair to both employer and employee.
Structure and order8 Centralisation and decentralisation: set decision authority at the level the situation needs. 9 Scalar chain: an unbroken line of authority from top to bottom. 10 Order: materials and people each in their proper place.
People and team spirit11 Equity: kindness joined with justice. 12 Stability of tenure: low turnover so people can learn their jobs. 13 Initiative: freedom to propose and carry out plans. 14 Esprit de corps: unity and team spirit.

Back to the bank branch. The assistant's problem breaks principle 4, unity of command. The fix is to agree who gives her orders, and to have the other manager route requests through that person.

The scalar chain and the gang plank. The scalar chain keeps every message on the line of authority. When that is too slow, Fayol's gang plank lets two people at the same level deal with each other directly, with their superiors' knowledge.

Fayol also divided an enterprise's activities into six groups: technical, commercial, financial, security, accounting and managerial. The last is the one he analysed.

Don't confuse unity of command with unity of direction. Unity of command is about a person: one boss each. Unity of direction is about an activity: one plan and one head for each group of activities with the same objective. A firm that makes both scooters and tractors keeps each line under its own head and its own plan.

Where it breaks. The principles are general and sometimes pull against each other. Division of work can make jobs dull, which undercuts initiative. Matrix organisations deliberately give people two bosses, breaking unity of command. Herbert Simon, in "The Proverbs of Administration" (1946), argued that such principles come in contradictory pairs, like proverbs, and do not say which to apply when.

In practice. Use the list to diagnose. Two bosses giving clashing orders points to unity of command. Slow approvals point to the scalar chain, and a gang plank may help. High staff turnover points to stability of tenure.

For exams. Expect to match principle numbers to descriptions, and to tell unity of command from unity of direction. Know the gang plank and the six groups of activities.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Your sales team in Pune needs a credit approval from finance before every large order. The request goes up to the sales head, across to the finance head and down to a credit officer, and takes three days. A gang plank would let the sales executive call the credit officer directly. The condition is the one Fayol set: both heads agree in advance and are kept informed. What will you do if the credit officer refuses an order the sales head wanted?

Centralisation is a dial, not a switch. Fayol's principle 8 asks where decisions should sit for this situation. A chain of pharmacies may centralise buying to get better prices and decentralise staff rosters to each store. The Organisation structure chapter in this unit takes this further.

Links. Theories of management (this unit) places Fayol in the classical school, beside Taylor and Weber.

blocks.title: Taylor's scientific management
blocks.html:
Two workers in a Pune auto-parts plant do the same job. One finishes 40 pieces a shift and the other 25, each taught by a different senior, and nobody knows which method is better. F. W. Taylor's answer was to stop guessing and measure.

In plain wordsScientific management means studying each job to find the best way to do it, training people in that way, and paying for results.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition, usually credited to Taylor: scientific management is the art of knowing exactly what you want people to do, and seeing that they do it in the best and cheapest way.

Taylor was an American engineer who worked in steel companies. He set out his approach in The Principles of Scientific Management (1911). He worked from the shop floor upward, replacing rule of thumb with measurement. His approach rests on seven elements:

  • Science, not rule of thumb: find the best method by study.
  • Harmony, not discord: managers and workers cooperate.
  • Scientific selection and training: the right person trained for the task.
  • Functional foremanship: several specialist foremen supervise each worker, one per kind of task, instead of one generalist supervisor. Taylor proposed eight: four in the planning department (route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian) and four on the shop floor (gang boss, speed boss, repair boss, inspector).
  • Differential piece-rate: a higher rate per piece for meeting the standard output, a lower rate for falling short.
  • Standardisation and simplification: uniform tools, methods and processes.
  • Time and motion study: break a job into steps, remove wasted movement, set an output standard.

Differential piece-rate, worked. Suppose the standard is 10 pieces a day, paid at ₹50 a piece for workers who meet it and ₹40 a piece for those who fall short. These figures are illustrative.

WorkerPieces madeRateDay's pay
Ravi11 (above standard)₹5011 × ₹50 = ₹550
Meena10 (meets standard)₹5010 × ₹50 = ₹500
Arjun9 (below standard)₹409 × ₹40 = ₹360

One piece fewer than standard costs Arjun ₹140 against Meena, far more than the ₹50 that piece would have earned. Taylor meant that gap to be a strong pull toward the standard.

Fayol and Taylor worked at the same time but started from opposite ends.

Point of comparisonFayol (administrative)Taylor (scientific)
Starting pointThe whole organisationThe individual task
Main concernHow to manage the organisationHow to perform work efficiently
Key ideasPrinciples, authority, unity, orderStudy, standards, incentives
ContributionAdministrative frameworkScientific work methods

Don't confuse time study with motion study. Motion study removes needless movements from a job. Time study then times the improved job to set the standard output. Also note the clash exams like: functional foremanship gives a worker eight bosses, which breaks Fayol's unity of command.

Where it breaks. Taylor treated workers mainly as people who respond to pay, and ignored their social needs. The Hawthorne studies, described in Theories of management (this unit), later showed how much those needs matter. Workers and unions resisted being speeded up. Repetitive, closely timed work can be dull and tiring. Functional foremanship was rarely adopted in full.

In practice. Taylor's tools live on in industrial engineering, standard work on assembly lines, and target handling times in call centres. Use them where the task is repetitive and measurable; use them carefully where judgement and goodwill matter more.

For exams. List the seven elements, name the eight functional foremen, work a differential piece-rate, and compare Taylor with Fayol.

blocks.title: Katz's three managerial skills
blocks.html:
The best salesperson in a branch is promoted to branch manager and struggles. She still sells better than anyone, but the new job asks for different skills. Robert Katz explained why.

In plain wordsA managerial skill is an ability you can learn and improve with practice, and it shows in what you do, not in what you could do.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a skill is an ability that can be developed, not necessarily inborn, and that shows in performance, not merely in potential. Katz (1955) named three skills every manager needs, in proportions that change with level.

SkillWhat it isWhere it weighs most
TechnicalKnowing the work: methods, tools, procedures and specialised knowledge, such as selling, accounting or engineeringFirst-line managers; its weight falls as one rises
HumanWorking with and through people: leading, motivating, communicating and resolving conflictEvery level; the main emphasis in middle management
ConceptualSeeing the organisation as a whole, how its parts depend on each other and on the environment, and connecting strategy to its partsTop management; its weight rises with level

An illustration. In an auto-parts plant, a shift supervisor needs to know how each machine runs and how to fix a jam (technical). The plant head needs to settle a row between the production and quality teams and keep both motivated (human). The managing director needs to judge whether the shift of customers to electric vehicles will make some parts obsolete (conceptual).

Emphasis shifts with rank. Lower management leans on technical skill, middle management on human skill with a balance of all three, and top management on conceptual skill. Managers also draw on related skills: communication, decision-making, delegation, planning, problem-solving and time management. Skills, unlike talent, can be learnt and improved with practice.

Don't add a fourth skill to Katz's list. Design skill is not one of Katz's three. Koontz and Weihrich later added it: the ability to solve problems in ways that benefit the enterprise. Katz's three are technical, human and conceptual.

Where it breaks. The level pattern is a broad tendency, not a rule. The owner of a small firm needs all three skills at once. In technology and knowledge firms, senior managers often still need deep technical skill. The three skills also overlap: resolving a conflict between two departments uses both human and conceptual skill.

In practice. Use the model to plan someone's development. A new supervisor promoted from the shop floor usually has technical skill and must build human skill. A middle manager moving up needs conceptual skill, which job rotation and cross-department projects help to build.

For exams. Know the three skills, which level each weighs most at, and that human skill matters at every level. A common trap lists design skill as one of Katz's.

blocks.title: Mintzberg's managerial roles
blocks.html:
Ask a manager to describe her job and she will say planning, organising and controlling. Watch her for a day and you see phone calls, short meetings, interruptions and quick choices. Henry Mintzberg studied that gap.

In plain wordsA managerial role is a set of actions people expect from someone because of the position they hold.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: managerial roles are specific actions or behaviours expected of and shown by a manager. Mintzberg named ten, in three groups.

Mintzberg watched five chief executives at work, one week each: at a consulting firm, a school system, a technology firm, a consumer-goods maker and a hospital. He reported in The Nature of Managerial Work (1973). Instead of orderly planning he found brief, varied and fragmented activity.

CategoryRoleWhat the manager does
InterpersonalFigureheadPerforms ceremonial and symbolic duties: greeting visitors, signing documents, presiding at functions
InterpersonalLeaderDirects, motivates, trains and counsels subordinates
InterpersonalLiaisonKeeps a network of contacts inside and outside the organisation
InformationalMonitorSeeks and receives information about changes, opportunities and problems
InformationalDisseminatorPasses information on to members of the organisation
InformationalSpokespersonSpeaks for the organisation to outsiders
DecisionalEntrepreneurStarts improvement projects and initiates change
DecisionalDisturbance handlerTakes corrective action in disputes and crises
DecisionalResource allocatorDecides who gets what: money, people, time and equipment
DecisionalNegotiatorRepresents the unit in negotiations with unions, suppliers, customers and government

One day at a bank branch, an illustration. The branch manager opens a new ATM (figurehead) and coaches a new clerk (leader). She meets the local traders' association (liaison) and reads a circular from the regional office (monitor). At the morning huddle she shares it with staff (disseminator). Later she answers a local reporter's questions (spokesperson). She starts a doorstep-banking trial for elderly customers (entrepreneur) and settles a customer's complaint about a failed transfer (disturbance handler). She decides which officer handles the loan queue (resource allocator) and agrees the renewal of the branch's lease with the landlord (negotiator).

The groups connect. Formal authority and status give rise to the interpersonal roles. These give the manager access to information (the informational roles), which the manager then uses to decide (the decisional roles).

Don't mix up the three informational roles. Direction tells them apart: the monitor brings information in, the disseminator passes it around inside, and the spokesperson sends it outside. Likewise, the leader role faces subordinates, while the liaison role faces people outside one's own chain of command.

Where it breaks. Five chief executives over five weeks is a small sample. Later studies broadly support the picture of fragmented work, but the time spent in each role varies with level and organisation. In practice the roles overlap; one meeting can involve several at once.

For exams. Expect "which role?" questions built on a short description, and the three groups with their members. Remember the ten as 3, 3 and 4.

Go deeper for practitioners

Folklore and fact. In a 1975 Harvard Business Review article, "The Manager's Job: Folklore and Fact", Mintzberg reported that half of the chief executives' activities lasted less than nine minutes. He argued that managers prefer live, spoken information to written reports. The picture of the calm planner, he said, was folklore.

Roles or functions? Mintzberg offered his roles as a challenge to the classical functions of planning, organising and controlling. Many textbooks now treat the two as compatible: the functions say what managers are trying to achieve, and the roles describe how they actually spend their time.

Roles and skills. The interpersonal roles draw mostly on Katz's human skill. The entrepreneur and resource allocator roles draw on conceptual skill. A manager weak in one skill will struggle in the matching roles.

A decision. A new store manager finds her days eaten by interruptions and has no time for the plan to cut wastage. Mintzberg would say the interruptions are the job. Which of them could a deputy handle, and which, such as the disturbance handler role, should stay with her?

text: The Gītā argues that each person performs best in the work that fits their own nature, and that taking up another's task is riskier. A modern reader will see specialisation. The traditional varṇa reading is contested, so treat this as a statement about fit between person and task.
pairings.quote: “Better one's own duty, imperfectly done, than another's duty done well.” श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । śreyān svadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmāt svanuṣṭhitāt. Bhagavad Gītā 3.35; also 18.45–47

text: Kauṭilya ties the ruler's own wellbeing to the wellbeing of those ruled. Power is held against an obligation to deliver results for others.
pairings.quote: “In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare, his welfare.” प्रजासुखे सुखं राज्ञः प्रजानां च हिते हितम् । prajāsukhe sukhaṃ rājñaḥ prajānāṃ ca hite hitam. Arthaśāstra 1.19.34

pairings.modern: Unity of direction, esprit de corps
text: The closing hymn of the Ṛgveda asks for shared movement, shared speech and a single purpose, which is Fayol's one plan and one team spirit.
pairings.quote: “Move together, speak together, let your minds be of one accord.” सं गच्छध्वं सं वदध्वं सं वो मनांसि जानताम् । saṃ gacchadhvaṃ saṃ vadadhvaṃ saṃ vo manāṃsi jānatām. Ṛgveda 10.191.2; common purpose at 10.191.4

text: Kauṭilya names sustained effort as the root of prosperity. The Gītā describes the ideal doer as combining resolve with enthusiasm (utsāha).
pairings.quote: “The root of wealth is activity; its absence brings ruin.” अर्थस्य मूलमुत्थानमनर्थस्य विपर्ययः । arthasya mūlam utthānam anarthasya viparyayaḥ. Arthaśāstra 1.19.35; Bhagavad Gītā 18.26

text: The Gītā defines yoga in terms of work done skilfully, which is close to Taylor's concern with doing a task the best way.
pairings.quote: “Yoga is skill in action.” योगः कर्मसु कौशलम् । yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam. Bhagavad Gītā 2.50

pairings.modern: Piece-rate and the fruit of action
text: Piece-rate ties reward to output. The Gītā tells the worker to commit fully to the action while not clinging to its reward. These work at different layers: the first is how a firm designs pay, the second is the worker's inner stance toward results. A firm can do the first and still invite the second.
pairings.quote: “You have a claim on action alone, never on its fruits.” कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana. Bhagavad Gītā 2.47

pairings.classic: leading by example, seeing the whole
text: The Gītā notes that people copy those they regard as best, which is human skill working through example. It also describes the clear kind of knowledge as seeing one undivided reality in all beings, which parallels conceptual skill.
pairings.quote: “Whatever the best person does, others do too.” यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः । yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 3.21; see also 18.20

text: Fayol's equity asks for fair treatment of all. The Gītā describes the wise as seeing a learned person, a cow, an elephant and an outcast with the same regard, and as even-minded toward friend and foe.
pairings.quote: समदर्शिनः । sama-darśinaḥ. “Those who see with equal regard.” Bhagavad Gītā 5.18; 6.9

chapters.title: Functions of Management
chapters.scope: Planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating and controlling: what each involves, step by step.

blocks.title: The functions of management
blocks.html:
A new manager takes over a bank branch on Monday. Nobody hands her a list of tasks, yet her week has the same shape as every manager's: decide what to do, arrange it, find the people, lead them, and check the results.

In plain wordsThe functions of management are the main kinds of work every manager does, in any organisation and at any level.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: management functions are the general duties managers carry out in almost every organisation. The most widely used list is Koontz and O'Donnell's: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.

Writers have listed the functions differently. Exams often ask whose list is whose.

WriterFunctions
Henri Fayol (1916)To forecast and plan, to organise, to command, to co-ordinate and to control
Luther Gulick (1937)POSDCORB: planning, organising, staffing, directing, co-ordinating, reporting and budgeting
George R. TerryPlanning, organising, actuating and controlling
Koontz and O'DonnellPlanning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling: the most widely used list

The five functions repeat in a cycle. Planning sets objectives and the course of action. Organising arranges tasks, people and resources. Staffing recruits, selects and develops people. Directing leads, motivates and communicates. Controlling measures results, compares them with the plan and corrects the gap, which feeds the next round of planning.

An illustration. A college fest committee plans the date, a budget and a footfall target. It organises sub-committees for sponsorship, stage and food. It staffs them with volunteers and briefs them. The convenor directs: she keeps people going and settles clashes. After the fest, the committee controls: it compares spending and footfall with the plan. Its lessons shape next year's plan.

Coordination runs through all five, which is why many writers call it the essence of management rather than a separate function. The functions overlap and are performed together, at every level. Top managers spend more of their time planning and organising; first-line managers spend more of theirs directing.

Don't confuse the lists' words. Fayol's "command" and Terry's "actuating" cover broadly what Koontz and O'Donnell call directing. Staffing appears in Gulick's and Koontz and O'Donnell's lists, but not in Fayol's or Terry's. Nor functions with roles: functions say what a manager is trying to achieve; Mintzberg's roles, in the chapter on management, describe how the day is actually spent.

Where it breaks. The neat sequence is a teaching device. Real managers plan, direct and control in the same hour, and Mintzberg's observation of managers found brief, fragmented activity rather than orderly steps.

For exams. Expand POSDCORB, match each list to its writer, and know why coordination is called the essence of management.

Plan, organise, staff, direct, control, then round again.

blocks.title: Planning
blocks.html:
A Pune auto-parts maker wins an order that doubles its output from next April. If it starts buying machines and hiring people in March, it will miss the order. The work that has to start now is planning.

In plain wordsPlanning is deciding today what will be done later, how, when and by whom.

Exam definitionPlanning is deciding in advance what to do, how to do it, when to do it and who is to do it (Koontz and O'Donnell).

Planning bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to be. M. E. Hurley put it in a line: planning is deciding in advance what is to be done. It is the primary function, since the others follow from it and controlling has nothing to measure without it.

Nature. Planning is goal-oriented, all-pervasive (done at every level), forward-looking, continuous, an intellectual process, and a matter of choice among alternatives. It offsets uncertainty, gives direction, reduces waste, guides decisions, helps coordination and makes control possible.

Classified byTypes
LevelCorporate, divisional, functional
FocusStrategic: long-term, for the whole organisation. Tactical: turns strategy into departmental plans. Operational: day-to-day. Contingency: a fallback ready if conditions change.
TimeLong-term, medium-term, short-term

The planning process has eight steps. The third column follows a kirana store planning its Diwali season; the figures are illustrative.

StepWhat happensA kirana store before Diwali
1. Recognise the need for actionScan for opportunities and problems, often with a SWOT analysisLast Diwali, sweets and dry fruit ran out in three days
2. Set objectivesFor the organisation, then for each departmentSell ₹10 lakh of goods in the festive fortnight
3. Develop planning premisesAssumptions about the future: external (economy, policy, technology, competition) and internal (resources, policies, management)Demand peaks in the last five days; the wholesaler gives 30 days' credit
4. Identify alternativesList the possible courses of action, then narrow them to the promising fewStock up early on credit; tie up with a sweet shop; take phone orders for home delivery
5. Evaluate alternativesWeigh each against the objectives: cost, risk, returnEarly stock ties up cash; home delivery needs a helper
6. Select an alternativeChoose the best, sometimes combining parts of severalStock up on credit and add phone orders
7. Formulate supporting plansDerivative plans such as hiring, training and budgets that make the main plan workHire two helpers; plan cash for paying the wholesaler
8. Implement and follow upAct through policies, procedures, budgets and rules, and check progressCheck sales against the target every evening

The owner also keeps a contingency plan: a second wholesaler, in case the first runs short.

Don't confuse planning with forecasting. A forecast estimates what will happen, such as Diwali demand. Planning decides what to do about it. Forecasts feed the planning premises. Nor a premise with an objective: a premise is an assumption about conditions; an objective is the result you aim for.

Where it breaks. A plan is only as good as its premises, and the future can prove them wrong. Detailed plans take time and money, can make an organisation rigid, and can give a false sense of security. In a fast-changing market, long-range detail dates quickly.

In practice. Write down the premises you are least sure of, and keep a contingency plan for each.

For exams. Expect the order of the eight steps, the meaning of planning premises, the types of plans, and why planning is the primary function.

Go deeper for practitioners

Kinds of plans. Koontz and Weihrich list plans from the broadest to the most specific: purposes or missions, objectives, strategies, policies, procedures, rules, programmes and budgets.

Policy, procedure, rule. A policy guides thinking in decisions and leaves room for judgement: "we prefer to promote from within". A procedure sets the order of steps for a task, such as the steps for approving a loan. A rule requires or forbids one specific action and leaves no judgement: "no smoking in the store". A budget is a plan stated in numbers.

Standing and single-use plans. Policies, procedures and rules are standing plans, used again and again. Programmes and budgets are usually single-use: drawn up for one purpose, such as the Diwali season, and then retired.

Links. Decision making (this unit) covers step 6, choosing among alternatives, in depth. Strategic intent (Unit 6) covers vision, mission and objectives.

blocks.title: Organising
blocks.html:
A chai stall that grows to three outlets can no longer run on the owner's memory. Someone must buy the milk, someone must count the cash, and everyone must know whom to ask. Organising settles who does what.

In plain wordsOrganising is dividing the work, grouping it, and deciding who does each part and who answers to whom.

Exam definitionOrganisation is the process of identifying and grouping the work to be performed, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships for the purpose of enabling people to work most effectively together in accomplishing objectives (Louis A. Allen).

Organising brings together physical, financial and human resources and sets up productive relationships among them to reach goals. Planning decides what to do; organising decides how it will be done. It settles what tasks there are, who does them, how they are grouped, who reports to whom and where decisions are made (Robbins and Coulter).

The organising process has four steps. The third column follows the owner of the three chai outlets.

StepWhat happensThree chai outlets
1. Identify activitiesList everything that must be done: bookkeeping, selling, training, quality controlBuy milk, tea and sugar; make tea; serve; collect cash; keep accounts; clean
2. Group activitiesCombine related activities into departments or units (departmentalisation)Buying and accounts at the centre; making, serving and cash at each outlet
3. Assign duties and authorityGive each position its tasks and the authority to carry them outEach outlet head runs the counter and may order snacks locally
4. Establish reporting relationshipsSet who reports to whom, so each person knows their authority and accountabilityHelpers report to the outlet head; outlet heads report to the owner

Benefits. Organising gives clear roles and accountability, and channels of communication. It uses resources without duplication, coordinates diverse work, and builds a structure that can grow. The result of organising is the organisation structure, the subject of a later chapter in this unit.

Don't confuse organising with staffing. Organising creates the positions and the links between them. Staffing fills those positions with people. Nor organising with the organisation: organising is the process; the organisation structure is what it produces.

Where it breaks. A structure drawn for today can become rigid tomorrow. Too many levels slow decisions down. People also form informal links that no chart shows, and work often flows through them.

For exams. Know the four steps in order, Allen's definition, the term departmentalisation, and the planning-what, organising-how contrast.

Identify, group, assign, relate.

blocks.title: Staffing
blocks.html:
A new bank branch opens with a building, computers and a deposit target, but only half its officers. Every other function stalls until the right people are in place.

In plain wordsStaffing is finding the right person for each job, then training, paying, rating and moving people so the jobs stay well filled.

Exam definitionStaffing is manning the organisation structure through proper and effective selection, appraisal and development of personnel to fill the roles designed into the structure (Koontz and O'Donnell).

Staffing fills the positions in the organisation structure and keeps them filled: the right person in the right job. Today it is largely the work of human resource management.

StepWhat happens
1. Manpower planningEstimate how many people, and of what kind, are needed (workload and workforce analysis)
2. RecruitmentFind prospective employees and encourage them to apply
3. SelectionChoose from the applicants: screening, tests, interviews, medical examination
4. Placement and orientationPut each person in the job they suit; orientation (induction) introduces them to colleagues, rules and facilities
5. Training and developmentBuild skills for the present job and for future roles
6. CompensationFix wages, salaries, incentives and fringe benefits
7. Performance appraisalRate performance against set standards
8. Promotion, transfer and career planningMove people to where they are best used, and plan their growth

An illustration, with round figures. A Pune auto-parts plant adds a production line that needs 40 operators.

  • Manpower planning: 10 operators can move across from an older line, so the plant needs 40 − 10 = 30 new people.
  • Recruitment: advertisements, visits to local ITIs and employee referrals bring in 300 applications.
  • Selection: screening, a skills test, interviews and a medical examination leave 30, one in ten applicants.
  • Placement and orientation: each joins a shift and spends the first day learning the safety rules and meeting the team.
  • Later steps: training on the new machines, fixing pay, a first appraisal after six months, and a path to shift leader.

Don't confuse recruitment with selection. Recruitment widens the pool: it attracts as many suitable applicants as possible. Selection narrows it: it rejects most of them to choose the few who fit. Nor placement with orientation: placement puts a person in a job; orientation introduces them to the organisation.

Where it breaks. Fayol's and Terry's lists do not name staffing separately, and some writers fold it into organising. In large firms the HR department runs the process. Yet every manager still staffs: choosing team members, training them and appraising them.

For exams. Know the eight steps in order and the difference between recruitment and selection. Unit 2's chapters on human resource planning, recruitment and selection, training and development, and compensation treat these steps in depth.

Plan, find, choose, place, grow, pay, rate, move.

blocks.title: Directing and leadership styles
blocks.html:
Two supervisors at the same plant get the same plan, the same machines and equally skilled workers. One shift meets its target and the other does not. The difference lies in how each one leads the shift, day by day.

In plain wordsDirecting is the daily work of guiding people, keeping them motivated and keeping them informed, so that the plan actually happens.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: directing (also called leading) is guiding, influencing, motivating and supervising people so that they work toward the organisation's goals.

Directing turns plans into action. It has four elements:

  • Supervision: overseeing the work.
  • Motivation: encouraging effort with monetary and non-monetary incentives.
  • Communication: passing on information and understanding.
  • Leadership: influencing people to follow.

How a manager directs depends on her leadership style.

StyleHow it worksStrengthWeakness
Autocratic (authoritarian)The leader decides alone and expects complianceFast decisions; a clear chain of commandStifles initiative and creativity; can raise turnover
Democratic (participative)The leader involves the team and keeps the final wordCommitment, creativity, moraleSlow; weak if members lack skill
Laissez-faire (free-rein)The leader provides resources and hands decisions to the groupSuits experienced, self-driven expertsUnclear responsibility; can lower productivity
TransactionalRewards and penalties for meeting set goalsClear, measurable targetsLittle room for innovation
TransformationalInspires change through a shared vision and personal exampleHigh morale and commitment to changeDepends heavily on the leader

One manager, three styles. At a bank branch on a busy month-end, the system goes down and the queue grows. The manager decides alone who handles which customers: autocratic, and right for a crisis. Next week she asks her staff how to rearrange the counters: democratic. Her most experienced loan officer she leaves to manage his own files: laissez-faire.

The first three styles come from Kurt Lewin's studies (1939). James MacGregor Burns (1978) set transactional leadership against transformational. Which style works best depends on the leader's personality, the followers and the organisation's culture.

Don't confuse directing with leadership. Leadership is one of directing's four elements; directing also includes supervision, motivation and communication. Nor transactional with autocratic: transactional describes a trade of rewards for results; autocratic describes who makes the decisions.

Where it breaks. Style labels describe tendencies, not fixed types. Most managers shift between styles, as the branch manager did, and no single style suits every situation.

For exams. Know the four elements, Lewin's three styles (1939) and Burns's pair (1978), and match each style to its strength and weakness. Unit 2's chapter on group behaviour and leadership covers the theories behind this.

Direct through people: oversee, encourage, inform, influence.

blocks.title: Coordinating
blocks.html:
During a Diwali sale, an electronics store's marketing team advertises a television offer. The warehouse has not stocked enough sets, and customers leave angry. Each team did its own job well; nobody fitted the jobs together.

In plain wordsCoordination is fitting everyone's work together so that it pulls in one direction, at the right time.

Exam definitionCoordination is the orderly arrangement of group effort to provide unity of action in the pursuit of a common purpose (Mooney and Reiley).

Because it runs through every function, Koontz and O'Donnell called coordination the essence of management rather than a separate function. Fayol listed it among his five elements, and it is the CO in Gulick's POSDCORB.

KindBetweenExample
InternalDepartments, units and people inside the organisationMarketing and the warehouse agree stock for an offer
ExternalThe organisation and outsiders: suppliers, customers, governmentThe store confirms delivery dates with its suppliers
VerticalLevels of the hierarchy, superior and subordinateA branch and its regional office agree targets
HorizontalDepartments at the same level, such as production and salesProduction plans output to match the sales forecast

How it is achieved. Clear objectives and plans, a sound structure with defined authority, effective communication, committees and liaison roles, good leadership, and voluntary cooperation among those involved.

Follett's four principles, applied to the Diwali sale:

  • Direct contact among the people concerned: the marketing and warehouse heads talk to each other, not through memos.
  • Early start, while plans are still being made: they agree stock before the advertisement is booked, not after it runs.
  • Reciprocal relating of all the factors in a situation: a change in the offer changes the stock, staffing and delivery plans too.
  • Continuity: they keep checking with each other throughout the sale, not just once.

Don't confuse coordination with cooperation. Cooperation is people's willingness to help each other. Coordination is the manager's deliberate work of arranging their efforts. Willing teams can still pull in different directions if nobody coordinates them.

Where it breaks. Coordination costs time: meetings, committees and reports. The bigger and more specialised an organisation becomes, the harder and more costly it is.

For exams. Know the Mooney and Reiley definition, why coordination is the essence of management, the four kinds, and Follett's four principles.

Many efforts, one direction.

blocks.title: Controlling
blocks.html:
A college fest committee budgets ₹5 lakh. Two weeks before the fest it has already spent ₹4.5 lakh, with the stage and lighting still unpaid. It finds out in time only because someone checked.

In plain wordsControlling is checking whether things are going to plan, and putting them right when they are not.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: controlling is measuring performance against standards, finding deviations and correcting them, so that goals are reached as planned.

Fayol wrote that control consists of seeing that everything is carried out in accordance with the plan adopted, the orders given and the principles laid down. Its object is to point out mistakes so that they may be rectified and prevented from recurring.

StepWhat happens
1. Set standardsMeasurable targets drawn from the plan: output, cost, quality, time
2. Measure performanceCollect data on what actually happened
3. Compare with standardsFind the deviation and its cause, attending to the significant deviations (management by exception)
4. Take corrective actionRemove the cause, or revise the standard or the plan if it was unrealistic

A worked example, with illustrative figures. A Pune plant's standard for the month is 10,000 pieces at ₹50 a piece, a budget of ₹5 lakh. It makes 9,000 pieces and spends ₹4.95 lakh.

  • Output: 9,000 against 10,000, so 1,000 pieces or 10% short.
  • Cost per piece: ₹4,95,000 ÷ 9,000 = ₹55, against a standard of ₹50. That is ₹5, or 10%, over.
  • Total spending looks ₹5,000 under budget. But 9,000 pieces should have cost 9,000 × ₹50 = ₹4.5 lakh, so the plant overspent by ₹45,000 for the output it made.

Both deviations are significant, so both go to the manager. The cause turns out to be a machine breakdown, and the correction is planned maintenance.

Nature. Control is continuous, present at every level, closely linked with planning, and action-oriented. Good control looks ahead to prevent deviations as well as back to correct them. Robert J. Mockler called it a systematic effort to compare performance with predetermined standards. It then takes whatever action is needed so that resources are used effectively and efficiently.

TechniqueWhat it checks
Personal observationWork seen first-hand
Reports and management information systemsRegular data on operations
Budgetary controlIncome and spending against the budget
Ratio analysis and return on investmentFinancial health and the return on capital
Break-even analysisThe output at which revenue covers cost
BenchmarkingPerformance against the best in the field

Don't confuse controlling with planning. Planning sets the standard; controlling checks against it, and its findings feed the next plan. Planning without controlling is pointless, and controlling without planning has nothing to measure. Nor control with punishment: its aim is to correct the cause, not to find someone to blame.

Where it breaks. Managers tend to measure what is easy to count, such as output, and miss what is hard, such as goodwill. Close control can make staff resentful. Some causes, such as a change in government policy or a strike at a supplier, lie outside the firm's control.

For exams. Know the four steps in order, management by exception, the techniques, and the link with planning.

Go deeper for practitioners

Control by timing. Robbins and Coulter sort controls by when they act. Feedforward control acts before the work, such as inspecting raw material as it arrives. Concurrent control acts during the work, such as a supervisor on the shop floor. Feedback control acts after it, such as the monthly report in the example above. Feedback comes too late for the month it measures, so the best systems add the other two.

A decision. Your plant misses its output standard three months running, and each time the cause is different. Step 4 offers two answers: remove the causes, or revise the standard. Before revising it, check whether the standard was ever met, and with what machines and staff.

Links. Strategy implementation and evaluation (Unit 6) applies the same loop to strategy.

text: The Kuṟaḷ describes the able ruler as one who can create resources, gather them, guard them and allocate what has been guarded. It names a cycle of duties rather than a single act, which is how the functions of management are taught. The couplet describes a king's work, not the modern list, so the link is a reading.

chapters.title: Theories of Management
chapters.scope: Five schools, each a response to the limits of the one before: efficiency, people, interconnection, situation, and quality with knowledge.

blocks.title: Classical school
blocks.html:
Ten machinists in a Pune auto-parts plant make the same bracket, each in his own way. Some make 60 a shift and some 90, and nobody knows which method is best. The classical school was built to answer questions like that.

In plain wordsThe classical school says management can be studied like engineering: find the best method for each task, set clear rules, and design the structure for efficiency.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: classical theory treats the organisation as a formal structure designed for efficiency, run on general principles that replace rule of thumb with systematic management.

PeriodLate 19th to early 20th century
Key namesF. W. Taylor, Henri Fayol
FocusEfficiency, structure and productivity

The school has three streams. Each looks at a different level of the organisation.

StreamKey nameLevel it studiesMain tools
Scientific managementF. W. Taylor, The Principles of Scientific Management (1911)The worker and the task on the shop floorTime and motion studies, standard tools and methods, scientific selection and training, differential piece-rate, functional foremanship
Administrative managementHenri Fayol (1916)The whole organisation, seen from the topFive functions of management; fourteen principles such as division of work, unity of command and scalar chain
BureaucracyMax WeberAuthority and rulesHierarchy of offices, written rules, merit (next block)

How the differential piece-rate works. Taylor paid a higher rate per piece to workers who reached a standard set by time study, and a lower rate to those who fell short. As an illustration, say the standard is 80 brackets a shift, paid at ₹6 a piece at or above standard and ₹5 below it.

  • A machinist who makes 90 earns 90 × ₹6 = ₹540.
  • One who makes 75 earns 75 × ₹5 = ₹375.
  • If the second machinist reaches 80, pay jumps to 80 × ₹6 = ₹480. Five more pieces bring ₹105 more.

The jump at the standard is the point: it gives a strong reason to learn the best method.

Don't confuse Taylor with Fayol. Taylor worked from the bottom up: one task, one worker, one best method. Fayol worked from the top down: what every manager does (planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling) and the principles for running the whole organisation.

Where it breaks. The school treated workers as economic beings moved mainly by pay, and ignored their social needs. Many workers and unions resisted time study as a speed-up. Fayol's principles came from experience, not testing. Herbert Simon later called such principles "proverbs", because pairs of them contradict each other.

In practice. Standard work, time standards on assembly lines and target handling times in call centres all come from this school. It suits routine, repeatable work.

For exams. Match each tool to Taylor or Fayol. Taylor is called the father of scientific management; Fayol, of administrative management.

blocks.title: Weber's bureaucracy
blocks.html:
Two people apply for the same trade licence at a municipal office. One knows the clerk; the other does not. In a bureaucracy as Max Weber described it, that should make no difference.

In plain wordsA bureaucracy runs on written rules and offices, so a decision depends on the rule, not on who asks or who decides.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: bureaucracy is a form of organisation marked by a hierarchy of offices, division of labour, written rules, impersonal relationships and appointment on merit.

Max Weber (1864–1920), a German sociologist, described bureaucracy as the most rational way to organise large-scale work. It rests on rational-legal authority: people obey rules and offices, not persons. Weber set it against two older kinds of authority.

Type of authorityPeople obey because…
TraditionalIt has always been so: custom and inherited position
CharismaticOf the leader's exceptional personal qualities
Rational-legalThe rule is lawful and the office holds the right to apply it
FeatureWhat it means
HierarchyA chain of offices, each supervised by the one above
Division of labourSpecialised roles with defined duties
RulesWritten, stable rules govern decisions
ImpersonalityDecisions follow rules, not personal feelings; the office belongs to the organisation, not its holder
MeritSelection and promotion by qualification, often tested in open competition
CareerA salaried career with a systematic pay structure
RecordsDecisions and actions are documented in files

An example. A public-sector bank branch handles a loan by the book. The customer fills a set form, the officer checks it against a list, and sanction limits rise with rank. As an illustration, the branch manager might approve loans up to ₹10 lakh, while larger ones go to the regional office. Every step is recorded in the file.

Weber's model is an ideal type: a pure model to compare real organisations against, not a description of any one office.

Strengths: predictability, fairness, accountability and efficiency in routine work; the model still shapes most governments. Weaknesses: rigidity, red tape, slow response to change, and routine that dulls initiative and leaves people feeling apart from the organisation's purpose.

Don't confuse Weber's bureaucracy with "bureaucracy" as an insult. In everyday speech the word means red tape. Weber meant a technically efficient form of organisation; red tape is what happens when it goes wrong.

Where it breaks. Robert Merton argued that staff trained to follow rules can come to treat the rules as ends in themselves. This is often called goal displacement. Bureaucracy also fits badly where work changes fast or needs judgement, a point the contingency approach takes up.

In practice. Use bureaucratic rules where fairness and consistency matter more than speed: recruitment, payroll, tax, examinations. Loosen them where people must adapt to each case.

The office, not the person; the rule, not the mood.

blocks.title: Neoclassical school
blocks.html:
Suppose a textile mill raises its piece rates, yet output stays flat. The workers have agreed among themselves what a fair day's work is. Pay alone did not move them.

In plain wordsThe neoclassical school says workers are people with feelings and friendships, and these shape how hard they work.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the neoclassical, or human relations, approach sees the organisation as a social system, in which workers' attitudes, group relationships and morale influence productivity.

Period1920s–1930s
Key namesElton Mayo
FocusHuman relations, motivation, communication, teamwork and morale

The Hawthorne studies (next block) found that productivity follows social and psychological factors, not physical conditions alone. Employees are social and emotional beings, so participative leadership and attention to relationships matter.

QuestionClassical viewNeoclassical view
What is a worker?An economic beingA social and emotional being
What moves output?Pay, methods and physical conditionsAlso attention, recognition, belonging and morale
Informal groupsIgnoredCentral: they set their own norms
LeadershipCommand and controlParticipation and listening

An example. A branch manager notices that a team's speed depends on one senior clerk whom everyone trusts. Instead of issuing a new rule, she asks him to help plan the change. That is the human relations idea at work: the informal leader matters as much as the formal one.

Many textbooks stretch the neoclassical label to a later behavioural science stream, from the 1950s. It includes McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y, covered below.

Don't confuse neoclassical management with neoclassical economics. In economics, "neoclassical" means the marginal analysis of Marshall and others. In management, it means the human relations school that followed Taylor and Fayol.

Where it breaks. A happy worker is not always a productive one: research finds a real but only moderate link between job satisfaction and performance. Critics also said the school neglected structure, technology and genuine conflicts of interest. Attention to feelings can slide into manipulation if nothing else changes.

For exams. Expect Mayo, the Hawthorne studies, and the shift from the economic worker to the social worker.

blocks.title: The Hawthorne experiments
blocks.html:
Engineers at a factory turned the lights down in a test room and waited for output to fall. It rose. Explaining why changed management thinking.

In plain wordsPeople often work differently when they know someone is watching or taking an interest.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the Hawthorne effect is the change in people's behaviour that results from knowing they are being observed or studied.

The Hawthorne studies (1924–1932) at the Western Electric Company's Hawthorne Works near Chicago began as engineering tests and ended as a finding about people. Elton Mayo, Fritz Roethlisberger and William Dickson led the later phases.

PhaseWhat it found
Illumination experiments (1924–1927)Output rose whether lighting went up or down, so physical conditions alone did not explain productivity
Relay assembly test room (1927–1932)A small group's output rose through changes in rest pauses and hours, and stayed high when the old conditions returned; attention, morale and the group mattered
Mass interviewing (1928–1930)About 20,000 interviews showed that workers valued being listened to, and that their attitudes shaped their work
Bank wiring observation room (1931–1932)The group set its own output norm and pressed members to keep to it, whatever the incentive

The lesson: workers are social beings. Informal groups, attention and recognition influence output as much as pay and physical conditions. The tendency of people to change their behaviour when they know they are being studied is now called the Hawthorne effect.

An everyday example. A regional manager announces a visit to a bank branch. That week the queues move faster and the files are tidier. Nothing about the work changed except that someone was watching.

Don't confuse the Hawthorne effect with the halo effect. The Hawthorne effect is about the people being observed: they change because they are watched. The halo effect is about the person judging: one good trait colours the rating of all the others.

Where it breaks. The test groups were tiny, a handful of workers in a room. Critics pointed out that the relay room also changed how the group was paid and replaced two workers, which could explain part of the rise. Later reanalyses of the original data found the effects smaller and less clear than first reported. The lasting contribution is the question the studies raised, more than their proof.

For exams. Know the four phases in order, with what each found. The findings were reported in Roethlisberger and Dickson's Management and the Worker (1939).

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. You pilot a new branch layout at one branch. Head office watches closely, staff know they are part of a trial, and service time falls by a fifth in a month. Before rolling it out to every branch, ask how much of the gain came from the layout and how much from the attention.

How to tell. Run the trial long enough for the novelty to wear off. Compare with a similar branch that also gets attention but not the new layout. Measure again after the observers leave.

Links. The bank wiring room's output norm is the same idea as group norms in the chapter on group behaviour (Unit 2). The interviewing programme is an early case of upward communication (Communication, this unit).

blocks.title: Theory X, Theory Y and Theory Z
blocks.html:
Two branch managers take over similar teams. One checks every file and every hour; the other sets targets and lets people plan their own day. Each is acting on a belief about what people are like.

In plain wordsTheory X and Theory Y are two opposite beliefs a manager can hold about people at work: X, that they must be pushed; Y, that they will commit if given the chance.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: Theory X assumes the average person dislikes work, avoids responsibility and must be directed and controlled. Theory Y assumes work is natural, and people direct themselves and seek responsibility when committed to objectives.

Douglas McGregor, in The Human Side of Enterprise (1960), argued that a manager's style follows from the manager's assumptions about people.

Assumption aboutTheory XTheory Y
WorkPeople dislike work and avoid itWork is as natural as play or rest
DirectionPeople must be coerced, controlled and threatenedPeople direct themselves toward goals they are committed to
ResponsibilityPeople avoid it and prefer to be ledPeople accept and seek it under the right conditions
Ambition and creativityLittle ambition; security matters mostImagination and creativity are widely spread
Resulting styleClose supervision, rewards and penaltiesParticipation, delegation and enriched jobs

Assumptions tend to prove themselves. A manager who assumes X watches closely and gives no room. People then wait to be told, which seems to confirm X. A manager who assumes Y gives room, and people who use it seem to confirm Y.

Theory Z names two later ideas. William Ouchi's Theory Z (1981) described a model drawn from Japanese management: long-term employment, collective decision-making, slow evaluation and promotion, and concern for the whole employee. Ouchi contrasted typical American firms (Type A) and Japanese firms (Type J), and called American firms with Japanese-style features Type Z. Earlier, Abraham Maslow (1969) had used the name for a dimension of work beyond Theory Y, concerned with meaning and self-transcendence.

Don't confuse Theory Y with having no control. McGregor's point was that people control themselves when they are committed to goals they share. Targets still matter; the question is who does the checking. And Theory Z is not McGregor's third step: it is Ouchi's separate model.

Where it breaks. McGregor offered assumptions, not tested findings. Neither theory fits every person or situation: a new, unskilled worker in a crisis may need clear direction. Ouchi's model was hard to transplant, and Japanese long-term employment applied mainly to core staff in large firms.

In practice. Check your own assumptions. Do you explain reasons, delegate whole tasks and ask for ideas? Or do you check every step?

For exams. Book and year (McGregor, 1960; Ouchi, 1981), and which assumption belongs to X or Y.

X controls, Y trusts, Z commits for the long term.

blocks.title: Systems approach
blocks.html:
A Pune auto-parts plant's sales team promises a big customer delivery in half the usual time. Production runs overtime, stores run short of steel, the wage bill rises and quality slips. One decision moved every department.

In plain wordsThe systems approach sees an organisation as parts that depend on each other and on the world outside, so a manager must look at the whole, not one piece.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a system is a set of interrelated and interdependent parts arranged to form a unified whole. An open system interacts with its environment; a closed system does not.

PeriodMid-20th century to present
Key namesChester Barnard, Ludwig von Bertalanffy

The organisation is an open system of interdependent subsystems (production, finance, HR and others) interacting with its environment. A change in one subsystem affects the rest. Key words: interdependence, integration, coordination, feedback, synergy. Think of the whole, not isolated parts.

Seen as a system, an organisation has five parts:

  • Inputs: materials, people, capital, information, technology.
  • Transformation process: work and management activities.
  • Outputs: products, services, financial and human results.
  • Feedback: results that shape the next inputs.
  • Environment: what the organisation draws from and serves.

Synergy means the whole achieves more than the parts could separately. A plant whose sales, production and stores plan together can promise dates it can keep. The same departments working apart cannot. Ludwig von Bertalanffy, a biologist, developed general systems theory; Chester Barnard described the organisation as a cooperative system. Daniel Katz and Robert Kahn applied open-system thinking to organisations in 1966.

Don't confuse the systems approach with the contingency approach. The systems approach says the parts connect and the environment matters. The contingency approach goes a step further: it asks which arrangement fits which situation. And don't confuse open with closed systems: the classical school, in effect, treated the organisation as closed.

Where it breaks. The approach is abstract. It tells you that everything connects, but not which link matters most or what to do. Managers found it easier to agree with than to apply.

In practice. Before a change, trace its effect on the other departments and on customers and suppliers. Cross-functional meetings and shared targets put the idea to work.

For exams. The five parts of a system, open and closed systems, synergy, and the names Barnard and Bertalanffy.

blocks.title: Contingency approach
blocks.html:
A rulebook that runs a steady assembly line well can choke a team designing a new electric scooter. The same method of managing gave opposite results in two places.

In plain wordsThe contingency approach says the right way to manage depends on the situation: if this, then that.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the contingency, or situational, approach holds that there is no one best way to manage; the right structure and style depend on situational factors such as the environment, technology, size and people.

Period1960s to present
Key namesFred Fiedler, Paul Lawrence, Jay Lorsch

There is no single best way to manage. Effectiveness depends on the fit between structure, environment, technology and people. The manager analyses the situation, adapts the approach, and improves results.

If the situation is…Then it usually suits…
A stable, predictable environmentClear rules, fixed roles, central decisions
A fast-changing, uncertain environmentFlexible roles, open communication, decisions close to the work
Routine technology, such as mass productionStandard procedures and closer supervision
A large organisationMore formal rules and specialised departments
Skilled, self-motivated peopleMore autonomy and less direct control

An example. A kirana store run by its owner needs no organisation chart: one person decides, on the spot. A retail chain with 200 stores needs written procedures, regional managers and a central buying team. Both are well run; each fits its situation.

Don't confuse the contingency approach with Fiedler's contingency model. The approach is a general view of management. Fiedler's model is one leadership theory within it: it matches a leader's style to how favourable the situation is. Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership is another.

Where it breaks. "It depends" is true but can be vague. The approach names many factors, but says little about how to weigh them when they pull in different directions. Measuring a situation, such as how uncertain an environment is, is itself hard.

In practice. Diagnose before you prescribe. Ask how stable the market is, how routine the work is, how large the unit is and how skilled the people are. Then choose the structure and style.

For exams. "No one best way" is the phrase to recognise; Fiedler, Lawrence and Lorsch are the names.

Go deeper for practitioners

The research behind it. Tom Burns and G. M. Stalker (1961) studied British firms and contrasted mechanistic structures, with rigid roles and central control, and organic ones, with flexible roles and lateral communication. Mechanistic structures suited stable conditions; organic ones suited changing markets and technology.

Joan Woodward (1965) studied manufacturing firms in England. She found that the structure of successful firms varied with their technology: unit and small-batch production, mass production, or continuous process production.

Paul Lawrence and Jay Lorsch (1967) showed that departments facing different environments become different from each other (differentiation). The more uncertain the environment, the more effort the firm needs to coordinate them (integration).

A decision. Your auto-parts plant runs its main line on tight procedures. It now sets up a small team to design parts for electric vehicles. Should the team follow the plant's procedures? The contingency answer is no: give it an organic structure, with fewer approvals and direct contact with customers. Keep the main line mechanistic, and appoint someone to link the two.

blocks.title: Contemporary approaches
blocks.html:
A Pune plant ships 1,000 brackets a day and finds 20 faulty at final inspection. Throwing them away fixes today's batch. Finding out why they fail fixes every batch after.

In plain wordsTotal Quality Management means everyone keeps improving the work, a little at a time, so customers get what they need. Knowledge management means making sure what people know is shared and used, not lost.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: TQM is a philosophy of management driven by continuous improvement and response to customer needs, involving every employee. Knowledge management is the systematic process of creating, sharing and using an organisation's knowledge to meet its goals.

PeriodLate 20th century to present
Key namesW. Edwards Deming, Peter Drucker, Ikujiro Nonaka

Two streams. Total Quality Management: continuous improvement and customer satisfaction through teamwork. Knowledge management: create, share and use knowledge so it becomes a competitive resource. Together they stress learning culture, innovation, adaptability, customer trust and employee contribution.

Quality. In the example, the defect rate is 20 ÷ 1,000 = 2%. Inspection only sorts good from bad after the work is done. TQM asks the people who make the brackets to find the cause, perhaps a worn tool, and fix the process. Deming taught these ideas to Japanese managers after the Second World War; the Japanese word kaizen is used for continuous improvement.

Knowledge. Some knowledge is explicit: it can be written down, as in a manual. Much is tacit: it lives in experience and is hard to put into words. Ikujiro Nonaka showed how firms create knowledge by turning one into the other and back. Peter Drucker coined the term "knowledge worker" for people who work mainly with what they know.

An example. A senior clerk at a bank branch knows which documents most often hold up loan applications. If she retires without passing it on, the branch loses that knowledge. A checklist she helps write makes it explicit; pairing her with a new officer passes on the rest.

Don't confuse TQM with inspection, or knowledge management with an IT system. Inspection catches defects after they happen; TQM prevents them and makes quality everyone's job. A database stores information; knowledge management is about people sharing and using what they know, much of it tacit.

Where it breaks. Many TQM programmes fade into forms and slogans when leaders lose interest. Small, steady improvements can miss the need for a big change. Knowledge databases go unused where people are not rewarded, or do not trust each other enough, to share.

For exams. Deming and PDCA, kaizen, tacit and explicit knowledge, Nonaka, and Drucker's knowledge worker.

blocks.title: From one school to the next
blocks.html:
Each school of management was a fix for the blind spot of the one before. Read in order, the five tell one story.

SchoolPeriodKey names
ClassicalLate 19th to early 20th centuryF. W. Taylor, Henri Fayol
Neoclassical1920s–1930sElton Mayo
Systems (modern)Mid-20th century to presentChester Barnard, Ludwig von Bertalanffy
Contingency1960s to presentFred Fiedler, Paul Lawrence, Jay Lorsch
ContemporaryLate 20th century to presentW. Edwards Deming, Peter Drucker, Ikujiro Nonaka

The sequence reads as a series of shifts: from tasks and structure to people; from people to the interconnected organisation; from one system to situation-specific management; and from adaptation to continuous improvement and knowledge.

Why each shift happened. The classical school made work efficient but ignored people, and the Hawthorne studies exposed that. The human relations school studied people but neglected structure and the world outside, which the systems view brought in. The systems view said everything connects but not what to do, so the contingency approach asked what fits where. Faster competition then put quality and knowledge at the centre.

One problem, five lenses. Customers complain about long queues at a bank branch.

  • Classical: study the steps of each transaction and remove the wasted ones.
  • Neoclassical: ask whether staff morale has dropped, and listen to them.
  • Systems: check whether a slow server at head office is holding up the counter.
  • Contingency: ask whether this branch, with its customers, needs a different set-up from the others.
  • Contemporary: measure waiting time weekly and improve it step by step, with staff ideas.

Don't read the schools as replacing each other. A modern firm uses time standards (classical), written rules (Weber), attention to teams (neoclassical), a view of the whole (systems), fit to circumstances (contingency) and quality cycles (contemporary) at once.

Where it breaks. The neat order is a teaching device. The dates overlap: Barnard's systems thinking, for example, appeared in 1938, a year before the main Hawthorne report was published.

For exams. Expect questions that ask you to put the schools in order, or to match a name or idea to its school.

Tasks, people, the whole, the situation, improvement.

pairings.classic: the Arthaśāstra as a management manual
text: Book 2 of the Arthaśāstra sets out superintendents (adhyakṣa) for separate departments such as agriculture, mines, trade, treasury and accounts, each with duties and checks. That is structure, specialisation and standard procedure written down roughly two thousand years ago.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra, Book 2 (Adhyakṣapracāra)

text: The peace invocation of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad is a teacher-and-student prayer for shared protection, shared nourishment and shared effort. The Gītā's portrait of the dear devotee begins with having no hatred toward any being, and with friendliness and compassion.
pairings.quote: “May we be protected together, nourished together, and work together with vigour.” सह नाववतु सह नौ भुनक्तु सह वीर्यं करवावहै । saha nāv avatu saha nau bhunaktu saha vīryaṃ karavāvahai. Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Brahmānandavallī (opening invocation); Bhagavad Gītā 12.13

text: The invocation of the Īśa and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads treats the part and the whole as inseparable. The Gītā describes a cycle in which beings and the forces of nature sustain each other: an open system with inputs, outputs and feedback.
pairings.quote: “That is whole, this is whole; from the whole the whole arises.” पूर्णमदः पूर्णमिदं पूर्णात्पूर्णमुदच्यते । pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyate. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1.1 “Nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.” परस्परं भावयन्तः श्रेयः परमवाप्स्यथ । parasparaṃ bhāvayantaḥ śreyaḥ param avāpsyatha. Bhagavad Gītā 3.11; cycle at 3.14–16

text: Classical Indian ethics is explicitly situational. The Gītā judges a gift by whether it is given in the right place, at the right time, to the right person, a three-part test that is the contingency principle in miniature.
pairings.quote: देशे काले च पात्रे च । deśe kāle ca pātre ca. “In the right place, at the right time, to the right recipient.” Bhagavad Gītā 17.20

text: Continuous improvement rests on repeated practice. The Gītā says an unsteady mind is brought under control through practice (abhyāsa) and detachment.
pairings.quote: अभ्यासेन तु कौन्तेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते । abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate. Bhagavad Gītā 6.35

text: The Gītā describes knowledge being transferred by humility, questioning and service, and calls knowledge the supreme purifier. Knowledge here is shared in relationship, not stored.
pairings.quote: “Learn it by humble approach, by questioning, by service.” तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया । tad viddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā. Bhagavad Gītā 4.34; 4.38

chapters.title: Communication
chapters.scope: The exchange of ideas, information and feelings between people or groups to reach mutual understanding.

blocks.title: What communication is
blocks.html:
A bank branch manager emails her team: "Please clear the pending files today." One officer clears the loan files. Another clears out the old records cupboard. The message was sent, but it was not understood.

In plain wordsCommunication is passing an idea from one person to another so that the other person understands it as it was meant.

Exam definitionCommunication is an exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or emotions by two or more persons (Newman and Summer).

The word comes from the Latin communicare, to share. It is the transfer of information and understanding from one person to another. Louis Allen calls it a bridge of meaning: a systematic and continuous process of telling, listening and understanding. Both definitions put understanding, not sending, at the centre.

Forms. Communication takes four forms: verbal, non-verbal, written and digital. In this list "verbal" means spoken. Strictly, written words are verbal too, as the block on oral and written communication explains.

Characteristics.

  • It is a two-way, continuous process: messages and replies keep flowing.
  • It needs at least a sender and a receiver.
  • It carries facts, ideas, opinions and feelings.
  • It is pervasive, found at every level and in every department, and goal-oriented.

Functions, shown in an auto-parts plant in Pune:

FunctionExample in the plant
InformA notice gives the new shift timings
InstructA supervisor shows a worker how to set a machine
Persuade and motivateThe plant head explains why a safety drive matters
IntegrateProduction, stores and dispatch meet each week to plan
CounselAn HR officer talks with a worker facing a personal problem
Hear grievancesA complaint about overtime pay reaches HR
TrainNew apprentices attend induction sessions

Done well, communication gives an organisation clarity, coordination, cooperation, better relationships and a shared sense of objectives.

Don't confuse communication with information. Information is the content, such as a notice on a board. It becomes communication only when someone receives it and understands it.

Where it breaks. The definitions describe a two-way exchange. Much of what organisations send is one-way: circulars, manuals, broadcasts. In these, nobody checks whether the reader understood, so the bridge of meaning may never be built.

For exams. Match each definition to its author: "exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or emotions" is Newman and Summer; "bridge of meaning" is Louis Allen. Know the four forms and the seven functions.

blocks.title: The communication process
blocks.html:
On a noisy shop floor in Pune, a supervisor shouts, "Torque it to forty." The worker hears "fourteen" and sets the machine wrong. Every step between the two of them was a chance for the message to change.

In plain wordsThe communication process is the chain of steps an idea passes through, from the sender's mind to the receiver's understanding and back.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the process in which a sender encodes a message and sends it through a channel to a receiver, who decodes it and returns feedback.

Seven steps.

  1. The sender forms an idea.
  2. The sender encodes it into words, gestures or visuals.
  3. The message carries information, ideas or emotions.
  4. It travels through a channel: spoken, written or electronic.
  5. The receiver takes it in.
  6. The receiver decodes it, making sense of it.
  7. Feedback returns to the sender and confirms understanding.

Noise is interference at any step. It comes in three kinds: physical (machine noise, a bad phone line), psychological (worry, anger, prejudice) and semantic (a word understood in a different sense). The goal is to minimise distortion and maximise understanding.
