Back to the shop floor. The idea was a setting of forty. The encoding was a shouted word. The channel was the air of a loud shop, so physical noise changed "forty" into "fourteen" before decoding. No feedback came back, so nobody caught the error. Two fixes close the gaps: write the setting on the job card, and ask the worker to repeat it back.

Don't confuse the medium with the channel. The medium is the broad means: spoken, written or electronic. The channel is the specific route the message takes, such as a phone call, a letter or an email. Face to face, feedback is immediate. In writing, the sender cannot see the receiver's face and must wait for a reply.

Where it breaks. A step-by-step model makes communication look like posting a parcel. In a real conversation both people send and receive at the same time, and the relationship between them colours every word. The models in the next block try to capture this.

For exams. Know the steps in order, the three kinds of noise, and that feedback is what closes the loop.

Encode, send, decode, reply.

blocks.title: Models of communication
blocks.html:
Two engineers read the same email and agree at once. A new trainee reads it and is lost. The words did not change; what each reader brought to them did. Models of communication try to show what is going on.

In plain wordsA communication model is a simple drawing of how a message gets from one person to another, and what can go wrong on the way.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a model of communication is a simplified representation of its elements and of the relations between them.

ModelYearWhat it adds
Shannon and Weaver1949A source, a transmitter (encoder), a channel, a receiver (decoder) and a destination, with noise distorting the signal. Built for telephone engineering, later applied to human communication; often called the mother of all models.
Schramm1954Communication as a two-way exchange: each party both encodes and decodes, and meaning is shared through an overlapping field of experience.
Berlo (SMCR)1960Source, message, channel, receiver, each shaped by factors such as communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture.

Each model adds something the last left out. Shannon and Weaver add noise. Schramm adds two-way exchange and shared experience. Berlo adds the human factors that shape each element.

Berlo in more detail. The source and the receiver are each shaped by communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture. The message is shaped by its content, elements, treatment, structure and code. The channel is one of the five senses: hearing, seeing, touching, smelling and tasting.

An example. Mumbai's dabbawalas mark each tiffin with a short code of letters, numbers and colours. To a dabbawala the code says where the tiffin goes. To an outsider it says nothing. The channel and the message are the same; the fields of experience are not.

Don't confuse a linear model with a two-way one. Shannon and Weaver draw a one-way line from source to destination. Schramm draws a loop in which both people send and receive.

Where it breaks. Shannon and Weaver's model measures how well signals travel, not whether meaning is shared. Berlo's SMCR, as usually drawn, shows neither feedback nor noise. Every model simplifies; each is useful for the question it was built to answer.

For exams. Match the model to its year and its key idea: noise (Shannon and Weaver, 1949), field of experience (Schramm, 1954), SMCR (Berlo, 1960).

blocks.title: Formal and informal communication
blocks.html:
A factory announces a cut in the festival bonus by circular on Monday. By the Saturday before, the canteen already knew, and had a version that was half wrong. The news travelled by two routes; only one was official.

In plain wordsFormal communication follows the official lines of the organisation. Informal communication follows people's personal links.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: formal communication passes through officially prescribed channels in the hierarchy; informal communication arises from social relationships outside those channels.

AspectFormalInformal
ChannelOfficial channels and the established hierarchyNatural, unstructured channels
StrengthConsistency, clarity, accountabilityRelationship building, quick exchange of ideas
ExamplesReports, memos, meetingsGrapevine, conversation, social media

Formal communication by direction:

  • Downward, for example circulars.
  • Upward, for example grievances.
  • Horizontal, between peers, for example joint forums.
  • External, for example annual reports.

Informal communication takes five common forms:

  • The grapevine: unofficial, fast, often inaccurate.
  • Face-to-face talk: direct, with instant feedback and non-verbal cues.
  • Social media: fast and flexible.
  • Telephone: immediate, but with limited visual feedback.
  • Non-verbal signals: gestures, posture and facial expression.

An example: a public-sector bank branch. Formal: a head-office circular on new rules for checking customers' identity; the branch manager's monthly report to the region; a meeting between the loans and deposits heads; the bank's annual report. Informal: a chat over tea, the staff's messaging group, and the grapevine on who is being transferred.

Don't confuse informal with spoken. The test is whether the channel is official, not whether words are spoken or written. A board meeting is spoken and formal. A message in a staff chat group is written and informal.

Where it breaks. Formal channels can be slow, and messages get filtered as they pass through levels. Informal channels cannot be controlled and can spread rumour. Neither works well alone.

In practice. Use formal channels for anything that must be recorded or binding. Listen to informal ones to sense mood and test ideas early. When a rumour spreads, a quick, clear formal statement takes away its fuel.

For exams. Expect to classify examples as formal or informal, and to name the four formal directions and the five informal forms.

blocks.title: Directions of communication
blocks.html:
A store-keeper notices that a supplier's parts are arriving late. The plant head hears about it three weeks later, when the line stops. The information existed; it could not travel upward fast enough.

In plain wordsThe direction of communication says who is talking to whom in the hierarchy: down, up, across, or across and up.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: communication in an organisation flows downward, upward, horizontally (laterally) or diagonally (crosswise) through its structure.

DirectionFlowsExamplesWatch for
DownwardFrom superiors to subordinatesOrders, policies, notices, job instructions, handbooksDelay, distortion and filtering through many levels; overload
UpwardFrom subordinates to superiorsReports, suggestions, grievances, complaintsFear of superiors, distortion, inattention at the top
Horizontal (lateral)Between people or departments at the same levelMeetings and memos between department headsRivalry between departments
Diagonal (crosswise)Between people at different levels in different departmentsA finance executive asks the marketing head directly for projected expensesBypasses the chain of command and unity of command

Each direction does a different job. Downward communication carries authority and objectives. Upward communication brings feedback, ideas and early warning. Horizontal communication coordinates. Diagonal communication saves time when speed matters.

In the plant. The plant head's safety circular goes down. The store-keeper's note on late parts should go up. The production and quality heads settle a schedule across. A quality inspector who phones the purchase manager about a faulty batch is communicating diagonally.

Don't confuse horizontal with diagonal. Horizontal is between people at the same level. Diagonal is between different levels in different departments. Fayol's gangplank is horizontal: peers talk directly, with their superiors' consent, and keep them informed.

Where it breaks. Upward communication is often the weakest, because people soften bad news before it reaches the top. Diagonal links are fast but can leave the managers in between uninformed.

In practice. Make upward flow safe: open-door hours, suggestion schemes, and meetings where senior managers hear directly from front-line staff. When people talk diagonally, ask them to copy their own managers.

For exams. Expect a short case asking you to name the direction. The diagonal example with the finance executive is a favourite.

blocks.title: Communication networks and the grapevine
blocks.html:
A rumour that the plant will close reaches 300 workers before lunch. The official notice denying it takes two days. A manager who knows how messages travel can use both routes, and not be surprised by either.

In plain wordsA communication network is the map of who talks to whom in a group.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a communication network is the pattern of channels among the members of a group.

NetworkPatternCharacter
ChainMessages pass up and down a line, as in the scalar chainOrderly, and follows the formal chain; slower, because each message passes through every link
WheelOne central person communicates with each member; members do not communicate directlyFastest for simple tasks; centralised
CircleEach person communicates with the two beside themSlow; no central leader
All-channel (free flow)Everyone communicates with everyoneHighest satisfaction and best for complex problems; no leader stands out, and the links multiply as the group grows

An example: a college fest committee. When the convenor phones each volunteer separately, the committee is a wheel. It works for quick tasks such as "who has the banners?" When the core team argues out the budget in one group chat, it is all-channel: slower to settle, but more ideas surface.

The grapevine is the informal network that grows from social ties. Keith Davis described four patterns along which it carries news.

PatternHow news spreads
Single strandEach person tells one other, in a line
GossipOne person tells everyone
ProbabilityEach person tells others at random
ClusterEach tells a few trusted people, who pass it on selectively; the most common pattern

The grapevine is fast and tells managers how people feel. It also carries rumour and distortion. It works best alongside open formal channels.

Don't confuse the grapevine with rumour. The grapevine is the channel. A rumour is unverified content that it sometimes carries. The grapevine also carries true news, often faster than the formal route.

Where it breaks. The classic network findings come from small groups solving set puzzles in a laboratory. Real organisations mix all four patterns, and change them from task to task.

For exams. Expect: which network is fastest for simple tasks (wheel), which gives the highest satisfaction (all-channel), and Davis's most common grapevine pattern (cluster).

Go deeper for practitioners

Where the findings come from. Alex Bavelas and Harold Leavitt ran the first network experiments around 1950. Groups passed notes along fixed channels to solve a simple puzzle. Centralised networks such as the wheel solved it fastest, and the person at the centre became the leader. Members at the edge were the least satisfied.

Complex tasks reverse the result. Later work, notably by Marvin Shaw, found that decentralised networks did better on complex problems. The person at the centre of a wheel becomes overloaded, which Shaw called saturation, while an all-channel group can share the thinking.

A decision. You lead a six-person project. For daily status updates, a wheel through you is efficient. For redesigning the product, open the channels so that everyone hears everyone. The mistake is to use one network for both.

blocks.title: Oral and written communication
blocks.html:
A branch manager tells a clerk on the phone to waive a ₹500 late fee for a customer. Months later an auditor asks who approved it. Nobody can prove anything, because nothing was written down.

In plain wordsOral communication uses spoken words. Written communication puts words on paper or on a screen.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: oral communication is the spoken exchange of messages, face to face or through a device; written communication is the exchange of messages in written or printed form.

AspectOralWritten
FormsFace-to-face talks, meetings, telephone, interviews, voice messagesLetters, memos, circulars, reports, manuals, notices, email
StrengthsQuick, flexible and personal; immediate feedback; saves time and costA permanent record and legal evidence; precise; fixes responsibility; suits long, complex or widely sent messages
WeaknessesNo record; easily misunderstood; poor for long messagesSlow, costly, impersonal and rigid; feedback is delayed

An example: a college fest committee. The convenor phones a caterer to bargain over the menu. Speech is quick, and both sides can adjust on the spot. Once they agree, she confirms the price, the date and the number of plates by email. If the caterer later disputes the bill, the email is the record.

Oral and written communication are both forms of verbal communication, because both use words. Non-verbal communication (gesture, expression, posture, tone, pictures and symbols) accompanies them. It often carries the feeling behind the words: the same "fine" can mean agreement or anger.

Don't confuse verbal with oral. Verbal means using words, spoken or written. Oral means spoken only. A letter is verbal but not oral. A nod is neither: it is non-verbal.

Where it breaks. Writing loses tone, so a short email can sound curt. Speech leaves no proof of what was agreed. Neither, on its own, tells the sender whether the receiver understood; that still needs feedback.

In practice. Discuss it, then write it down. Put policies, approvals and anything involving money or legal duties in writing. Give sensitive news in person first, and follow it up in writing.

For exams. Expect a case asking which form suits a message, and a question on why both oral and written communication count as verbal.

Say it for speed; write it to keep it.

blocks.title: Barriers to communication
blocks.html:
A head-office circular says: "All branches to ensure full KYC compliance by EOD." A new clerk does not know what EOD means. A worried manager reads it as a threat. The same words failed in two different ways.

In plain wordsA barrier is anything that stops a message from arriving, or from being understood as it was meant.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: barriers to communication are factors that block, distort or filter a message between sender and receiver.

BarrierWhat gets in the wayExample
PhysicalNoise, distance, poor infrastructureMachine noise on a shop floor; a call that keeps dropping
PsychologicalStress, fear, biasA worker afraid to report a mistake to an angry supervisor
LanguageVocabulary, jargon, dialectAn engineer's jargon used with a new apprentice
CulturalBeliefs, traditions, practicesStaff who will not disagree with a senior in public, so silence is read as agreement
PerceptualDifferent interpretations, experience, attitudesSales reads "cut costs" as fewer trips; finance reads it as fewer staff
OrganisationalRigid hierarchy, poor coordinationA suggestion that must pass through four levels before anyone acts
AttitudinalNegative behaviour, dominance, lack of respectA manager who interrupts and never asks for views

Semantic barriers, a kind of language barrier, are a frequent problem at work. They include one word with several meanings, poorly built messages, faulty translation, jargon and unstated assumptions. "EOD" in the circular is jargon; "full compliance" is an unstated assumption about what counts.

Overcoming barriers:

  • Clarify the idea before sending it.
  • Choose the right medium for the message.
  • Use simple language.
  • Listen actively.
  • Ask for feedback.
  • Keep channels open in every direction.

Rewritten, the circular might say: "Please finish identity checks on all customer accounts by 5 pm today. Call the regional office with any questions."

Don't confuse barriers with noise. Noise, in the process model, is interference at some step. Barriers are the sources of that interference. Physical noise comes from physical barriers; semantic noise comes from semantic barriers.

Where it breaks. The categories overlap: jargon is a language barrier and also a perceptual one, since experts and newcomers read it differently. A list names the barriers but does not say which matters most in a given case.

For exams. Expect to match examples to the seven types, and to recognise semantic barriers as a kind of language barrier.

text: A Ṛgvedic hymn compares the wise shaping speech with the mind to sifting grain through a sieve. That is encoding as a deliberate act. Another hymn says speech has four measured parts, three kept hidden and one spoken. Later grammarians, notably Bhartṛhari, developed this into stages running from the unspoken idea to uttered sound, which maps loosely onto idea, encoding and transmission.
pairings.quote: “Where the wise shaped speech with the mind, as grain is sifted with a sieve.” सक्तुमिव तितउना पुनन्तो यत्र धीरा मनसा वाचमक्रत । saktum iva titaünā punanto yatra dhīrā manasā vācam akrata. Ṛgveda 10.71.2; four parts of speech at 1.164.45

text: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad says the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and deeply absorbed; later Vedānta reads this as a three-stage path: listen, reflect, then assimilate. Understanding is completed by the listener's own work, as in decoding and feedback.
pairings.quote: श्रोतव्यो मन्तव्यो निदिध्यासितव्यः । śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ. “To be heard, reflected on, deeply absorbed.” Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5

text: The Gītā sets three tests for speech: it should not agitate, it should be true, and it should be pleasant and beneficial. Manu's formula pairs truth with pleasantness and cautions against an unpleasant truth. The Gītā's verse also includes the test of benefit.
pairings.quote: “Speech that causes no distress, that is true, pleasant and beneficial.” अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । anudvegakaraṃ vākyaṃ satyaṃ priyahitaṃ ca yat. Bhagavad Gītā 17.15; Manusmṛti 4.138

pairings.classic: the chain from anger to confusion
text: The Gītā traces how strong emotion distorts what a person hears and remembers: anger leads to delusion, delusion to loss of memory, and loss of memory to loss of judgement. It is a compact account of why stress, fear and bias block a message.
pairings.quote: क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ sammohāt smṛtivibhramaḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 2.63

chapters.title: Decision Making
chapters.scope: Selecting the best course of action from the available alternatives to reach a goal.

blocks.title: What a decision rests on
blocks.html:
A kirana store owner must decide by Friday whether to stock a new brand of atta. Waiting is also a choice, and it has a cost. Every manager's week is made of choices like this.

In plain wordsA decision is picking one option from at least two, to solve a problem or reach a goal.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a decision is the choice of one course of action from two or more alternatives to solve a problem or reach a goal. Trewatha and Newport, and George Terry, define it in close to these words.

Peter Drucker put its weight plainly: whatever a manager does, he does through making decisions.

Decisions rest on three foundations:

  • Logic: reasoning from what is known to what follows.
  • Analysis: breaking the problem down and examining the facts and figures.
  • Intuition: a judgement that comes from experience, faster than reasoning it out.

Back to the kirana store. Logic says that if customers keep asking for the brand, some will buy it. Analysis checks the numbers: how many asked last month, the margin per bag, and the shelf space it needs. Intuition is the owner's sense, from years at the counter, of whether her regulars will really switch.

Done well, decisions improve efficiency, effectiveness, adaptability, competitiveness and organisational performance.

Features. Decision making:

  • is a mental, rational process;
  • is selective, so there must be alternatives to choose from;
  • is purposive, aimed at a goal;
  • implies commitment until the decision is carried out;
  • involves evaluating both the alternatives and the results;
  • happens at every level;
  • can be negative: a choice not to act is still a decision.

Don't confuse decision making with problem solving. Problem solving is the whole effort to find and close a gap. Decision making is the point inside it where one option is chosen. And with only one option there is no decision, since nothing is selected.

Where it breaks. Each foundation has a weakness. Logic is only as sound as its starting assumptions. Analysis needs data and time, which a manager may not have. Intuition is fast, but it can carry habits and biases from situations that no longer apply.

For exams. Know the definition, Drucker's line, the three foundations and the features, especially that a decision needs alternatives and that not acting is a decision.

Logic, analysis, intuition.

blocks.title: Types of decision
blocks.html:
A bank branch manager approves a routine travel claim in a minute, then spends a month on whether to open a branch in a new district. Both are decisions, but they need very different handling.

In plain wordsA programmed decision has come up so often that a rule already exists for it; a non-programmed decision is new, and has to be thought through.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: programmed decisions are routine and repetitive, handled by set rules and procedures; non-programmed decisions are novel, complex and unstructured, needing judgement and creativity. The distinction is Herbert Simon's.

Decisions can be sorted in four ways.

Classified byTypes
ProgrammabilityProgrammed: routine, repetitive, handled by rules and procedures (travel approval). Non-programmed: novel and complex, needing judgement and creativity (launching a new product).
Management levelStrategic: long-term, high impact, tied to vision and mission. Tactical: mid-level, turns strategy into action. Operational: day-to-day execution.
PurposeRoutine: daily operations. Major: high risk, high return, long-term. Minor: low risk, limited consequences.
Decision makerIndividual: one person, quick. Group: discussion toward consensus. Personal: made outside an official role. Organisational: official decision affecting the institution.

One public-sector bank, many types.

  • Approving a travel claim within the rules: programmed, operational, routine.
  • Opening branches in a new district: non-programmed, strategic, major.
  • Turning that plan into a target and staff list for each new branch: tactical.
  • Which teller covers the counter at lunch: operational, minor.
  • A credit committee approving a large loan: a group, organisational decision.
  • The branch manager choosing to take an evening course: personal.

The four ways of sorting cut across each other, so one decision carries several labels at once.

Don't confuse programmed with minor. Programmability is about whether a rule exists, not about the stakes. A bank's standard home-loan approval is programmed, yet each loan involves lakhs of rupees. A one-off choice of venue for a staff picnic is non-programmed, yet minor.

Where it breaks. The categories have blurred edges. A programmed decision becomes non-programmed when conditions change and the old rule no longer fits.

In practice. Turn recurring decisions into rules, so that they can be delegated. That frees senior managers' time for the non-programmed ones, which usually rise to the top of the organisation.

For exams. Expect a case to classify. Programmed against non-programmed is the pair asked most often.

Programmed or not. Strategic, tactical or operational.

blocks.title: The rational decision process
blocks.html:
A manager who picks the first option that comes to mind may be lucky, but cannot explain or repeat the choice. The rational process makes a decision traceable, step by step.

In plain wordsA rational decision follows set steps, so that the best option is chosen for clear reasons.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: rational decision making is a step-by-step process of choosing the alternative that gives the greatest value, judged against stated criteria and within stated limits.

  1. Define the problem and its urgency.
  2. Gather information.
  3. Identify the criteria.
  4. Weight the criteria.
  5. Develop alternatives.
  6. Evaluate them against the criteria on feasibility, cost, risk and outcome.
  7. Choose the best balance of benefit and risk.
  8. Implement, by assigning responsibility and resources.
  9. Monitor results and correct where needed.

Short form: identify, inform, alternatives, evaluate, select, implement, review.

Worked example. A Pune auto-parts firm must choose a site for a new warehouse. Its criteria and weights are rent (40%), distance to its main customers (35%) and labour available (25%). Each site is scored out of 10, where higher is better: a high rent score means low rent. The scores are illustrative.

SiteRent (0.40)Distance (0.35)Labour (0.25)Weighted score
A8563.20 + 1.75 + 1.50 = 6.45
B5972.00 + 3.15 + 1.75 = 6.90
C9453.60 + 1.40 + 1.25 = 6.25

Site B wins, although its rent is the highest. Site C has the lowest rent but comes last, because distance carries heavy weight. Then the firm implements: it names a project head and a budget. Six months later it reviews whether delivery times actually fell.

Don't confuse criteria with alternatives. Criteria are what you judge by: rent, distance, labour. Alternatives are what you choose between: sites A, B and C. Set the criteria before scoring, or the favourite option tends to shape them.

Where it breaks. The model assumes full information, clear goals and time to compare every option. Herbert Simon argued that real managers have bounded rationality: limited information, time and mental capacity. So they satisfice: they choose the first option that is good enough, rather than search for the best.

For exams. Know the order of the steps and the short form, and that the process ends with monitoring, not with the choice.

Go deeper for practitioners

Simon's three phases. Simon also described decision making as intelligence (searching for problems that call for a decision), design (developing possible courses of action) and choice (selecting one). The nine steps above fit inside these three.

Sensitivity. Before trusting a weighted score, change the weights a little and see whether the winner changes. In the example, weight rent 50%, distance 25% and labour 25%. Sites A and C then score 6.75 each and site B 6.50, so B drops to last. A decision that flips on a small change in weights needs more thought, or more data.

A decision. Your team favours site C before any scoring is done. Ask each member to set and weight the criteria privately first, then compare. It is harder for the favourite to bend the weights once they are written down.

Links. Planning, in Functions of Management, uses the same core steps: alternatives, evaluation, selection. Groupthink, the main risk when a group decides, is covered in Group Behaviour, Teams and Leadership (Unit 2).

blocks.title: Techniques and tools
blocks.html:
A store owner choosing how much stock to buy, and a plant manager choosing which defects to fix first, face different kinds of decision. Each kind has a tool built for it.

The table pairs twelve common techniques with what each is best for.

TechniqueWhat it doesBest for
Decision treeMaps alternatives to possible outcomesRisk analysis
Delphi methodAnonymous expert rounds until consensus formsForecasting
Decision matrixScores options against weighted criteriaSelection
Cost-benefit analysisCompares expected costs with expected benefitsInvestment
PEST analysisPolitical, economic, social and technological factorsMarket entry
SWOT analysisStrengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threatsStrategy
Conjoint analysisMeasures how customers trade off product featuresProduct and pricing
Pareto analysisThe vital few causes behind most problems (80/20 principle)Quality improvement
Multi-votingNarrows a long list in rounds: each member gets votes equal to about a third of the items and spends them on the top prioritiesProject selection
Linear programmingOptimises output or minimises cost under constraintsProduction planning
Payback analysisTime taken to recover an investmentCapital decisions
Feasibility studyTechnical, financial and legal viabilityNew projects

Decision tree, worked. A kirana store plans a line of Diwali gift hampers. It can stock 200 or 100. The owner judges the chance of high demand at 0.6 and of low demand at 0.4. The payoffs are illustrative.

  • Stock 200: EV = 0.6 × ₹60,000 + 0.4 × (−₹20,000) = ₹36,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹28,000.
  • Stock 100: EV = 0.6 × ₹30,000 + 0.4 × ₹5,000 = ₹18,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹20,000.

Stocking 200 has the higher expected value. But it can lose ₹20,000, while stocking 100 never loses. An owner who cannot afford that loss may still choose 100.

Payback, worked. A chai stall buys a coffee machine for ₹1.2 lakh. It adds ₹4,000 a month in net cash. Payback = ₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹4,000 = 30 months, or two and a half years.

Pareto, applied. A bank branch sorts a year's customer complaints by cause. It may find that two causes, such as long queues and failed ATM withdrawals, account for most of them. Fixing those two first does the most good.

Don't confuse PEST with SWOT. PEST looks only outside the firm. SWOT looks inside (strengths and weaknesses) and outside (opportunities and threats). Nor the Delphi method with a meeting: Delphi experts never meet and answer anonymously, so no one voice dominates.

Where it breaks. A tool is only as good as its inputs: probabilities and scores are often guesses. Payback ignores everything earned after the investment is recovered, and treats a rupee next year as equal to a rupee today. The 80/20 split is a rule of thumb, not an exact law.

For exams. Match each technique to its use, and expect a short expected-value or payback calculation.

Match the tool to the decision.

text: Kauṭilya holds that every undertaking begins with deliberation, and lists five parts to it: the means of starting the work, the men and material available, the division of place and time, remedies against failure, and the accomplishment of the aim. That reads as a decision process: define, gather resources, schedule, manage risk, review results.
pairings.quote: मन्त्रपूर्वाः सर्वारम्भाः । mantrapūrvāḥ sarvārambhāḥ. “All undertakings are preceded by counsel.” Arthaśāstra 1.15.2; five limbs at 1.15.42

text: At the end of the Gītā, Kṛṣṇa lays out his teaching and hands the decision to Arjuna after full reflection. The process is advice, analysis, and a choice that remains the decider's own.
pairings.quote: “Reflect on this fully, then do as you wish.” विमृश्यैतदशेषेण यथेच्छसि तथा कुरु । vimṛśyaitad aśeṣeṇa yathecchasi tathā kuru. Bhagavad Gītā 18.63

text: The Gītā names five factors behind any action: the seat or base, the doer, the instruments, the effort, and circumstance beyond control. As an implementation checklist it covers location, people, tools, effort, and the uncertainty that remains.
pairings.quote: “The base, the doer, the various instruments, the many separate efforts, and providence as the fifth.” अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम् । विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् । adhiṣṭhānaṃ tathā kartā karaṇaṃ ca pṛthagvidham, vividhāś ca pṛthak ceṣṭā daivaṃ caivātra pañcamam. Bhagavad Gītā 18.14

pairings.classic: knowing what to do and what to avoid
text: The Gītā classifies the deciding faculty (buddhi) by quality. The clear kind distinguishes what should be done from what should not, what is to be feared from what is not, and what binds from what frees.
pairings.quote: प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च कार्याकार्ये भयाभये । pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca kāryākārye bhayābhaye. Bhagavad Gītā 18.30

text: The Yoga Sūtras describe a stage of concentrated insight called ṛtaṃbharā prajñā, which carries truth. It is a classical name for disciplined intuition, a different thing from a hunch.
pairings.quote: ऋतंभरा तत्र प्रज्ञा । ṛtaṃbharā tatra prajñā. Yoga Sūtra 1.48

pairings.classic: the seven elements of the state
text: Kauṭilya's account of the seven constituents of a state (ruler, minister, territory, fortress, treasury, army, ally) is an inventory of strengths and weaknesses, used before deciding whether to act. It works as an audit in the way SWOT does.
pairings.quote: स्वाम्यमात्यजनपददुर्गकोशदण्डमित्राणि प्रकृतयः । svāmy-amātya-janapada-durga-kośa-daṇḍa-mitrāṇi prakṛtayaḥ. Arthaśāstra 6.1.1

chapters.title: Organisation Structure
chapters.scope: The framework that defines roles, responsibilities, authority and communication, so resources align with goals and accountability is clear.

blocks.title: Types of structure
blocks.html:
StructureGrouped byStrengthChallenge
FunctionalSpecialised functionsEfficiency, specialisationFunctional silos
DivisionalProduct, geography or customerFlexibility, focusDuplication
MatrixDual reporting: function and project managerCollaborationDual authority
HierarchicalTop-down authorityClear authority, accountabilitySlow adaptation
VirtualDispersed teams linked by technologyFlexibility, cost efficiencyTechnology dependence
LeanFlat, waste eliminatedEfficiency, autonomyManagerial overload
HybridA combination of the aboveAdaptabilityComplexity

Informal and flexible forms: network (fluid relationships, agile), flat (few management levels, fast communication), holacracy (self-managed teams and circles, collective decisions), team-based (cross-functional teams, goal-oriented) and boundaryless (reduced internal and external barriers, partnerships).

blocks.title: Line, line-and-staff and other forms
blocks.html:
FormHow it worksStrengthWeakness
Line (scalar, military)Authority runs straight down a single chain from top to bottomSimple, clear, quick decisions, strict disciplineNo specialists; key managers overloaded
Line-and-staffLine managers command; staff specialists advise and serve them (general staff assist an executive, specialist staff give expert advice, service or control)Expert advice while unity of command is kept; used by most large firmsConflict between line and staff; staff advise without answering for results
Functional (F. W. Taylor)Grew from Taylor's functional foremanship: specialist foremen each direct the same worker on their own functionExpertise at every pointBreaks unity of command; confusing for workers
CommitteeA group of managers decides jointly on matters referred to itPooled judgement; decisions accepted more readilySlow and costly; responsibility diluted
ProjectA temporary team drawn from several departments for one time-bound goal, disbanded at the endFocus and speed on complex one-off workUncertain careers; conflict over shared people

Mechanistic and organic structures (Tom Burns and G. M. Stalker, 1961): a mechanistic structure has rigid rules, centralised decisions, narrow spans and vertical communication, and suits stable conditions; an organic structure has few rules, decentralised decisions, wide spans and lateral communication, and suits a changing environment.

Formal and informal organisation. The formal organisation is deliberately designed: official positions, rules and the chart. The informal organisation grows on its own from friendships and social groups, communicates through the grapevine, and can support or undermine the formal one. Wise managers work with it.

blocks.title: Authority, responsibility and accountability
blocks.html:
Authority is the right to give orders, make decisions and use resources. Herbert Simon called it the power to make decisions that guide the actions of others. Responsibility is the obligation to perform the duties assigned. Accountability is answering to a superior for the results. Authority flows downward; responsibility and accountability flow upward.

TheorySource of authority
Formal (classical)Position and ownership: it flows down from the top through the hierarchy
Acceptance (Chester Barnard, 1938)The subordinates who accept it: an order has authority only if it is accepted. Orders within a person's zone of indifference are accepted without question
CompetencePersonal knowledge and skill that others defer to, whatever the position

Kinds of authority: line authority to command, staff authority to advise, and functional authority, a specialist's right to direct a particular activity in other departments.

Parity of authority and responsibility. Authority should match responsibility (Fayol's second principle; Urwick's principle of correspondence). Authority without responsibility invites misuse; responsibility without authority leaves a person unable to act. Authority is used within the limits set by the organisation's policies, not by personal preference.

Absoluteness of responsibility. A manager can delegate authority, and the subordinate becomes responsible for the task, but the manager's own ultimate responsibility and accountability to the superior cannot be passed on.

blocks.title: Span of control and charts
blocks.html:
Wide spanNarrow span
ShapeMany subordinates per manager, fewer levelsFew subordinates per manager, more levels
GainsFaster decisions, lower managerial cost, greater autonomyClose supervision, better coordination
CostsManager overload, limited supervisionSlower decisions, higher cost, bureaucracy

An organisational chart shows who reports to whom. Four common charts are hierarchical (top to bottom), flat (few levels, broad span), matrix (dual reporting) and divisional (separate business units); a team-based chart maps cross-functional teams.

The organising process runs from purpose and goals, through inputs (materials, information, resources), activities and tasks, to outputs (products, reports, services), with monitoring and a feedback loop that drives improvement.

blocks.title: How wide a span: Graicunas and Urwick
blocks.html:
V. A. Graicunas, in "Relationship in Organization" (1933), showed why a span cannot grow without limit. A manager with n subordinates deals not only with each of them but with groups of them and with the relations between them. The number of possible relationships is:

R = n [2n−1 + n − 1]
Subordinates (n)Possible relationships (R)
11
26
318
444
5100
6222
7490
81,080

Subordinates grow one at a time while relationships grow exponentially: adding a seventh subordinate more than doubles them. Lyndall Urwick drew the rule that no superior can directly supervise the work of more than five, or at most six, subordinates whose work interlocks.

What sets the right span: the subordinates' competence and training; how simple, similar and standardised the work is; how clear the plans and delegation are; how fast conditions change; communication technology; how spread out the people are; the manager's other duties; and the degree of decentralisation. Spans are usually narrower at the top and wider at the operating level. Removing levels to widen spans is called delayering.

blocks.title: Delegation and decentralisation
blocks.html:
Delegation passes responsibility and authority for a task from superior to subordinate. Responsibility is the duty to do the work, authority is the power to decide, and accountability is answering for results. The superior keeps ultimate accountability. A sound delegation provides training, guidance, trust and feedback. Short formula: responsibility, authority, action, accountability.

Decentralisation spreads decision-making power systematically across the organisation and can be functional, geographic, product- or service-based, or market-based.

DelegationDecentralisation
MeaningSpecific authority transferredAuthority systematically distributed
ScopeNarrowBroad
LevelA task, an individualThe organisation, a unit
FocusResponsibility and supervisionAutonomy and distribution

Memory hook: delegation is about the person; decentralisation is about the system.

blocks.title: Centralisation and decentralisation
blocks.html:
Louis A. Allen defined centralisation as the systematic and consistent reservation of authority at central points, and decentralisation as the systematic effort to delegate to the lowest levels all authority except what can only be exercised at central points. No organisation is wholly one or the other; it is a matter of degree. Ernest Dale's tests of the degree: how many decisions are made lower down, how important they are, how many functions they cover, and how little they need to be checked above.

CentralisationDecentralisation
MeritsUniform policies and action; tight control; no duplication of specialists across branches; suits small firms and emergenciesLighter load on top management; faster, local decisions; develops future managers; suits large, diversified firms; better morale
DemeritsOverloads the top; slow decisions; stifles initiative and morale lower downCostlier, with duplicated functions; harder coordination and control; conflict between units

Factors that decide the degree: the size and spread of the organisation; the cost and importance of decisions; the need for uniform policy; top management's philosophy; the availability of capable managers lower down; control techniques and information systems; and how quickly the environment changes. Decentralisation is delegation extended systematically through every level.

text: Kauṭilya argues that no ruler can govern alone. Sovereignty needs helpers, so appoint counsellors and listen to them. This is the case for delegation, with the listening that makes it work.
pairings.quote: “Kingship is possible only with assistance; one wheel alone does not move.” सहायसाध्यं राजत्वं चक्रमेकं न वर्तते । sahāyasādhyaṃ rājatvaṃ cakram ekaṃ na vartate. Arthaśāstra 1.7.9

text: Manu prescribes a layered administration: an officer over one village, one over ten, one over twenty, one over a hundred and one over a thousand. Each tier reports to the one above it, a description of scalar chain and span.
pairings.quote: Manusmṛti 7.115–117

text: Book 2 of the Arthaśāstra assigns each domain (treasury, mines, trade, agriculture, accounts) to its own head, with defined duties and audit. This is a functional structure.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra, Book 2

text: The Atharvaveda speaks of the sabhā and samiti as two deliberative assemblies, daughters of Prajāpati. They are group bodies where decisions were made by discussion, which a modern reader may compare to self-managed circles. The comparison is loose: these were assemblies of a polity.
pairings.quote: सभा च मा समितिश्चावताम् । sabhā ca mā samitiś cāvatām. Atharvaveda 7.12.1

text: The Gītā's wheel of sacrifice has inputs, transformation, outputs and a return, and says whoever refuses to turn it lives in vain. As a picture of purpose, input, activity, output and feedback, it parallels the organising process.
pairings.quote: “Whoever here does not keep turning the wheel thus set in motion…” एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः । evaṃ pravartitaṃ cakraṃ nānuvartayatīha yaḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 3.14–16

chapters.title: Business Economics and Demand
chapters.scope: Economic theory applied to business decisions, and the study of why and how much people buy.

blocks.title: What business economics is
blocks.html:
A kirana store owner has ₹50,000 to spend. She could stock a new brand of atta, buy a second fridge, or keep the cash for the festival rush. Each choice rules out the others, and none comes with a guaranteed result.

In plain wordsBusiness economics uses the ideas and tools of economics to help a firm make better choices.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: business economics is the application of economic principles and methods to real business situations, to inform decisions on production, pricing, investment and risk management.

The terms business economics and managerial economics are used for the same subject. The next concept gives its classic definitions.

At the kirana store, an illustration. Economics turns the owner's worry into four questions she can work on.

DecisionAt the storeThe economic questionThe tool
ProductionStock the new atta, and how much?How many packets will sell each week?Demand analysis and forecasting (this chapter)
PricingSell it ₹5 below the leading brand?How strongly will buyers react to the price?Elasticity of demand (next chapter)
InvestmentBuy the second fridge?Will extra cold-drink sales repay its cost, and what else could the money earn?Opportunity cost and investment appraisal
Risk managementWhat if the festival rush is weak?How likely is a bad season, and what would it cost?Forecasting a range, not a single number

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up. Suppose the same ₹50,000 could earn the owner ₹4,000 a year in extra stock. Then that ₹4,000 is a real cost of the fridge, though no account will show it.

Don't confuse business economics with accounting. Accounting records what has already happened, in rupees paid and received. Business economics looks ahead at choices, and it counts costs that appear in no account, such as the income given up.

Where it breaks. Economic models simplify. They assume that people choose rationally, that other things stay equal and that data exist. A small firm often has only the owner's judgement, so the tools frame the question more often than they settle it.

For exams. Treat business economics and managerial economics as one subject. Expect questions on its definition and on the decisions it serves: production, pricing, investment and risk management.

blocks.title: Managerial economics: nature, scope and importance
blocks.html:
The owner of an auto-parts plant in Pune must decide whether to add a second shift. Part of the answer lies inside the firm, in orders and costs. Part lies outside it, in interest rates and the car market.

In plain wordsManagerial economics is economic theory put to work on a manager's decisions and plans.

Exam definitionManagerial economics is the integration of economic theory with business practice for the purpose of facilitating decision-making and forward planning by management (Spencer and Siegelman, 1959).

It links economic theory with business practice. Writers have defined it in similar ways; exams ask you to match each definition to its author.

WriterManagerial economics is…
Joel Dean (1951), the first textbook on the subjectthe use of economic analysis in formulating business policies
Spencer and Siegelman (1959)the integration of economic theory with business practice for the purpose of facilitating decision-making and forward planning by management
McNair and Meriamthe use of economic modes of thought to analyse business situations
Edwin Mansfieldthe application of economic concepts and economic analysis to the problems of formulating rational managerial decisions
Brigham and Pappasthe application of economic theory and methodology to business administration practice

Nature.

  • Mainly microeconomic: it studies one firm. It uses macroeconomics, the study of the whole economy, to understand the environment the firm works in.
  • Normative: it says what the firm should do, not only what firms do.
  • Pragmatic and decision-oriented: it aims at an answer a manager can use.
  • Forward-looking under uncertainty: every decision concerns a future nobody knows.
  • Conceptual and quantitative: it draws on statistics, mathematics, operations research and accounting.

Scope. It has an inside and an outside.

SideCoversAt the Pune plant (an illustration)
Operational (internal, micro)Demand analysis and forecasting; cost and production analysis; pricing decisions and market structure; profit management, including break-even analysis; capital management and investment appraisalHow many parts will car makers order? What does a second shift cost? What price should the plant quote?
Environmental (external, macro)The economic system and government policy; national income, employment, saving and investment; the financial sector; foreign trade; labour and capital markets; and the social and political settingWill interest rates rise? Is the car market growing? Could a change in policy cut demand?

Why it matters. It applies theory to real problems: what to produce, how much, by which technique, at what price, and where to invest. It supports forecasts of demand, cost and price, and it helps a firm plan for an uncertain environment.

Objectives. The traditional assumption is profit maximisation. Firms may pursue other goals: sales revenue (William Baumol), growth (Robin Marris), or a satisfactory level of performance rather than the maximum (Herbert Simon's satisficing).

Don't confuse normative with positive economics. A positive statement describes what is, and can be tested, such as "a 10% price rise cuts sales by 15%". A normative statement says what should be done, such as "so we should not raise the price". Managerial economics uses positive analysis to reach normative advice.

Where it breaks. Profit maximisation is hard to apply. It does not say whose profit, or over which period: this year's or the next ten years'. Managers also lack full information, which was Simon's point.

For exams. Match each definition to its writer, and remember Joel Dean (1951) for the first textbook. Sort topics into operational and environmental scope. Pair Baumol with sales, Marris with growth and Simon with satisficing.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why firms may not maximise profit. In a large company the owners (shareholders) and the managers are different people. Adolf Berle and Gardiner Means described this separation of ownership and control in 1932. Managers may then pursue size, sales or security.

Baumol's model has the firm maximise sales revenue, subject to a minimum profit that keeps shareholders content. Marris's has it maximise its rate of growth. Simon argued that people with limited information and time look for a solution that is good enough, which he called bounded rationality.

A decision. The Pune plant is offered a large order at a thin margin. A profit maximiser accepts only if the extra revenue exceeds the extra cost. A sales maximiser accepts if total profit stays above the minimum. Before you apply a rule, ask which objective the owners actually hold.

blocks.title: How economics has been defined
blocks.html:
A college fest committee has ₹2 lakh. A band costs ₹1.5 lakh and food stalls ₹1 lakh, so it cannot have both. Is economics about raising more money, about people's well-being, or about choosing well? Each famous definition gives a different answer.

In plain wordsEconomics studies how people and societies use limited resources to meet their wants.

Exam definitionEconomics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses (Lionel Robbins, 1932).

Five writers, over about 170 years, put the weight on five different things.

WriterYearEmphasisIdea
Adam Smith1776WealthNature and causes of the wealth of nations; wealth creation.
Alfred Marshall1890WelfareStudy of ordinary business of life; human welfare.
Lionel Robbins1932Scarcity and choiceHuman behaviour as a relation between ends and scarce means with alternative uses.
J. M. Keynes1936Income and employmentWhat determines a whole economy's income, output and employment; the foundation of macroeconomics (The General Theory).
Paul Samuelson1948Resources, choice and growthHow resources are produced, distributed and consumed; integrated micro and macro view.

Robbins applied to the fest. The ends are many: music, food, decoration. The means, ₹2 lakh, are scarce and have alternative uses. If the committee books the band, the food stalls it gives up are the opportunity cost of that choice.

How each answered the one before. Smith's book, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, put wealth at the centre. Marshall moved the focus to people: economics studies mankind in the ordinary business of life, and the material requisites of well-being. Robbins objected that "material" leaves out services, such as a teacher's or a doctor's, which are scarce and paid for. Robbins's own definition says little about unemployment, which Keynes made central in 1936, or about growth, which Samuelson's definition includes.

Don't confuse Marshall's "welfare" with the welfare state. Marshall meant material well-being: income and the things it buys. He was not writing about government benefits.

Where it breaks. No single definition covers all that economists now study. Modern textbooks usually combine them: scarcity and choice at the core, with the whole economy and growth added.

For exams. Match writer, year and emphasis. The books are The Wealth of Nations (1776), Principles of Economics (1890), An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science (1932), The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) and Samuelson's Economics (1948).

Smith wealth, Marshall welfare, Robbins scarcity, Keynes employment, Samuelson growth.

blocks.title: Demand
blocks.html:
In a Diwali sale, a student wants a ₹60,000 phone but has ₹15,000. Her uncle could afford it but has no interest in phones. For the shop, neither of them is demand.

In plain wordsDemand is how much of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, over a period of time.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: demand is the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices during a given period, other things remaining the same.

Effective demand = desire + ability to pay + willingness to pay

A want becomes demand only when the buyer can pay and intends to. Demand also has a time period: 200 cups of tea a day is a different demand from 200 cups a month.

Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity. Quantity demanded is the amount bought at one specific price. That difference decides what a change is called.

What changedWhat happens on the graphWhat it is called
The good's own priceA movement along the same curveExpansion (price falls) or contraction (price rises) of quantity demanded
Any other determinantThe whole curve shiftsIncrease (shift to the right) or decrease (shift to the left) in demand

At a kirana store, an illustration. A brand of biscuits sells 100 packets a week at ₹20. If the price falls to ₹18 and sales rise, quantity demanded has expanded. If a new housing society opens nearby and sales reach 130 packets at the same ₹20, demand has increased: the curve has shifted.

Determinants of demand

  • Price of the good itself.
  • Income: for normal goods demand rises with income; for inferior goods it falls, as buyers move to better options.
  • Tastes and preferences.
  • Prices of related goods: a dearer substitute (coffee, for a tea drinker) raises demand; a dearer complement (petrol, for a two-wheeler) lowers it.
  • Expected future prices: if buyers expect a rise, they buy more now.
  • Population: more buyers, more demand.
  • Government policy, such as taxes and subsidies.

Don't confuse an increase in demand with an expansion of quantity demanded. Only a change in the good's own price moves you along the curve; everything else shifts it. Cost of production is a supply-side factor and does not determine demand. It can change the price, and so the quantity demanded, but it is not on the list.

Where it breaks. "Other things remaining the same" rarely holds in a real market. Prices, incomes and tastes change together, so a firm finds it hard to tell a movement from a shift in its own sales data.

For exams. Expect "which of these shifts the demand curve?" A change in the good's own price never does. Also expect the three parts of effective demand.

blocks.title: The demand function
blocks.html:
A snack stall's sales depend on its price, but also on the weather, the stall next door and payday. To forecast sales or test a price, a manager writes all of these down in one line.

In plain wordsA demand function is a formula that links the quantity demanded to the things that drive it.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the demand function states the functional relationship between the quantity demanded of a good and its determinants.

In its simplest form, demand depends on the good's own price, Dx = f(Px). In full:

Dx = f(Px, Pr, Y, T, E, N, A)

Here Px is the good's own price, Pr the prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), Y income, T tastes and preferences, E expectations of future prices and income, N population, and A advertising. A demand schedule lists quantities at different prices; the demand curve graphs it.

A linear demand function has a constant slope. Take Q = 50 − 2.5P, and read it as a snack stall's plates sold per day at a price of ₹P (an illustration). Each ₹1 rise in price cuts sales by 2.5 plates, at every price.

Price (₹)WorkingPlates a dayElasticity, 2.5 × P ÷ Q
1850 − 2.5 × 18 = 50 − 45545 ÷ 5 = 9
1650 − 2.5 × 16 = 50 − 401040 ÷ 10 = 4
1250 − 2.5 × 12 = 50 − 302030 ÷ 20 = 1.5
1050 − 2.5 × 10 = 50 − 252525 ÷ 25 = 1
450 − 2.5 × 4 = 50 − 104010 ÷ 40 = 0.25

Elasticity here is (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q), with the minus sign ignored. ΔQ ÷ ΔP is 2.5 everywhere on this line, so only P ÷ Q changes. Elasticity falls as one moves down a straight demand line.

A non-linear demand function has a changing slope, such as Q = aP−b. Its elasticity is constant at b, at every price.

Don't confuse slope with elasticity. Along the straight line above, the slope never changes, but elasticity (2.5 × P/Q) is 9 at P = 18 and 1.5 at P = 12. Slope compares raw changes; elasticity compares percentages.

Where it breaks. Firms estimate real demand functions from past data, usually by regression (see Demand forecasting). The estimates hold only while buyers, rivals and incomes stay much as they were.

For exams. Expect to substitute a price into a linear function, or to name each variable in Dx = f(Px, Pr, Y, T, E, N, A).

blocks.title: Law of demand
blocks.html:
When a sweet shop cuts its prices in a Diwali sale, the queue grows. Few rules in business are as reliable as this one.

In plain wordsWhen a good gets cheaper people buy more of it, and when it gets dearer they buy less, if nothing else changes.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: other things being equal, the quantity demanded of a good varies inversely with its price.

Other things equal, when price falls quantity demanded rises, and when price rises it falls. "Other things equal" means that income, tastes, the prices of related goods and expectations stay as they were.

Price per packetPackets sold a week
₹2560
₹20100
₹15150

The table is an illustration of a demand schedule. Plot it, and the line falls from left to right.

Why the curve slopes downward.

  • Income effect: a lower price raises real purchasing power, so buyers can afford more.
  • Substitution effect: the good becomes cheaper relative to alternatives, so buyers switch towards it.
  • Diminishing marginal utility: each extra unit is worth less to the buyer, so buyers pay less for more (see Utility analysis).

Textbooks often add two more reasons. At a lower price new buyers enter the market, and the good is put to more uses, as when cheaper electricity is used for cooling as well as light.

Don't confuse the law of demand with elasticity. The law gives only the direction: price up, quantity down. Elasticity, the next chapter, measures how far quantity moves.

Where it breaks. A few goods break the law (the next concept). In real sales data, other things are rarely equal, so a price cut and a shift in demand often arrive together.

For exams. Learn the three reasons. The income effect and the substitution effect together make up the price effect; indifference curve analysis is the usual tool for separating them.

Price down, quantity up, other things equal.

blocks.title: Exceptions and special demand effects
blocks.html:
A jeweller raises the price of a limited range and sells more pieces, not fewer. A very poor family pays more for rice and ends up buying more rice. Both seem to break the law of demand.

In plain wordsAn exception is a case where people buy more of a good when its price rises.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: exceptions to the law of demand are cases in which the quantity demanded rises with a rise in price, so the demand curve slopes upward.

EffectCore ideaExample
VeblenHigher price raises status, so demand risesLuxury cars
GiffenPrice rises, demand rises, because a strong income effect outweighs substitution for an inferior goodStaple foods
SnobExclusivity: demand rises with uniqueness and falls as others buyLimited-edition watches
BandwagonOthers buy, so the consumer followsTrending smartphones

Two further exceptions: speculative goods (a buyer who expects prices to rise buys more now) and necessities (demand is very inelastic, so a price rise barely cuts purchases). A high price can also be read as a sign of quality.

How a Giffen good works, an illustration. A very poor household must buy 10 meals' worth of food a day with ₹70. Rice costs ₹4 a meal; dal and vegetables cost ₹10 a meal. It buys 5 meals of each: ₹20 + ₹50 = ₹70.

Now rice rises to ₹5 a meal. The same 5 and 5 would cost ₹25 + ₹50 = ₹75, more than the household has. To still eat 10 meals, it gives up one meal of dal and buys 6 of rice: ₹30 + ₹40 = ₹70. Rice became dearer, and the household bought more of it.

A Giffen good needs three conditions together: it is strongly inferior, it takes a large share of the budget, and it has no close substitute. Then a price rise makes buyers so much poorer that they buy more of it. Marshall named the case after Sir Robert Giffen, who is credited with observing it among poor households. Veblen described conspicuous consumption in The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899). Harvey Leibenstein named the bandwagon, snob and Veblen effects in a 1950 paper.

Don't confuse a Giffen good with a Veblen good. A Giffen good is a cheap staple of the poor, driven by the income effect. A Veblen good is a luxury of the rich, driven by status. Every Giffen good is inferior, but most inferior goods are not Giffen goods.

Where it breaks. Several items on the list are not true exceptions. With necessities, quantity still falls a little: the curve is steep, not upward-sloping. With speculation, expectations have changed, so the curve has shifted. Bandwagon and snob effects mainly change how strongly market demand reacts to price. Real Giffen goods are rare. Robert Jensen and Nolan Miller (2008) found evidence of Giffen behaviour for rice among very poor households in Hunan, China, in a field experiment that subsidised rice.

For exams. Match each effect to its idea and example. For Giffen goods, remember the three conditions and the income effect; for Veblen goods, status and The Theory of the Leisure Class.

Veblen: status. Giffen: staple. Snob: exclusive. Bandwagon: follow.

blocks.title: Types of demand
blocks.html:
A Pune firm makes brake pads. Nobody wants brake pads for their own sake: its sales rise and fall with the car market. Knowing what kind of demand a firm faces tells it what to watch.

In plain wordsDemand can be grouped by who is buying, how goods are linked, and how long buyers have to adjust.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition of the key type: derived demand is the demand for a good that arises from the demand for another good it helps to make or use.

TypeMeaningExample
Individual and marketOne consumer's demand; all consumers' demand added together at each priceOne family's milk; a whole town's milk
Firm and industryOne company's sales; all firms in the industry togetherOne cement brand; all cement sold
JointDemand for goods used togetherCar and petrol
CompositeDemand for a good with several usesElectricity
DerivedDemand that depends on demand for another goodSteel for cars
DirectDemand for final consumption, also called autonomous demandFood, clothing
IndependentDemand unaffected by other goodsSalt
Short-run and long-runDemand before and after buyers have time to adjust; long-run demand is usually more elastic, as buyers find substitutesPetrol this month; petrol over five years
Durable and non-durableDurable goods last, can be postponed, and are partly bought as replacements; non-durable goods are bought again and againA refrigerator; bread

Market demand, worked, an illustration. At ₹60 a litre, three families buy 2, 1 and 3 litres of milk a day. Market demand at that price is 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 litres. Repeat at every price and you have the market demand curve.

The brake-pad maker faces several types at once. Its demand is derived from car sales. Part of it is replacement demand from cars already on the road. Its own sales are firm demand; all brake-pad makers together make up industry demand.

Don't confuse joint demand with composite demand. Joint demand is two goods wanted together for one purpose (a car and petrol). Composite demand is one good wanted for several purposes (electricity for lights, fans and machines).

Where it breaks. The types overlap. Electricity is composite demand, and for a factory it is also derived demand. Few goods are truly independent of all others.

In practice. A firm facing derived demand watches its customers' markets, not only its own. A firm selling durables watches the age of goods already in use, because replacements make up part of its sales.

For exams. Expect to match an example to its type: car and petrol is joint, electricity composite, steel for cars derived, salt independent.

blocks.title: Demand forecasting
blocks.html:
A cement dealer must order stock months before the building season. Order too little and customers go to a rival; order too much and cash sits in the godown. A forecast of demand is what the order rests on.

In plain wordsDemand forecasting is making a careful, reasoned estimate of how much will sell in a future period.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: demand forecasting is the estimation of the future demand for a product, under given conditions, so that the firm can plan.

In the short run it guides production, pricing, sales targets and working finance. In the long run it guides capacity, investment and manpower planning.

Steps: set the objective, fix the period, choose a method, collect primary or secondary data, then estimate and interpret.

MethodHow it worksWatch for
Survey of buyers' intentionsAsk consumers what they plan to buy: a complete census, a sample survey, or the end-use method (forecast demand from the industries that use the product)Costly; intentions are not purchases
Collective (sales-force) opinionSalespeople estimate demand in their territories, and the estimates are added upBias toward their own sales quotas
Expert opinion and DelphiExperts give estimates; in the Delphi method they answer anonymously in rounds, seeing a summary of the others' views, until their estimates converge (developed at RAND in the 1950s)Slower than a single meeting; depends on the experts
Market experimentsTest marketing under real but controlled conditions, varying price or promotionCostly and slow; competitors may react
Trend projectionFit a trend to past sales, by free hand, moving averages or least squares (Y = a + bT), and extend itAssumes the past pattern continues
RegressionEstimate demand from its determinants: Y = a + bX, or multiple regression with several variablesNeeds good data on each determinant
Barometric methodUse leading indicators that move before demand, such as building permits ahead of cement demand, with coincident and lagging indicators as checksA good leading indicator is hard to find

A trend projection, worked, an illustration. The cement dealer sold 40, 44, 50, 54 and 62 thousand bags in five years. Number the years T = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, so that they add to zero.

a = ΣY ÷ n = 250 ÷ 5 = 50  ·  b = ΣTY ÷ ΣT² = 54 ÷ 10 = 5.4

Here ΣTY = (−2 × 40) + (−1 × 44) + 0 + (1 × 54) + (2 × 62) = −80 − 44 + 54 + 124 = 54. And ΣT² = 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10. The trend is Y = 50 + 5.4T. Next year is T = 3, so the forecast is 50 + 5.4 × 3 = 66.2 thousand bags.

Survey methods suit new products and the short run; statistical methods suit established products with long sales records. No method is free of error, so forecasts are often cross-checked.

Don't confuse a forecast with a sales target. A forecast estimates what will sell. A target states what management wants sold. Setting the forecast equal to the target hides the gap that management needs to see.

Where it breaks. Every statistical method assumes the future resembles the past. A new rival, a change in policy or a sudden shock breaks the pattern, and the trend line will not see it coming.

In practice. Forecast a range, not a single number, and record each forecast so its error can be measured later.

Go deeper for practitioners

Moving averages. A three-year moving average smooths out one-off years. For the dealer: (40 + 44 + 50) ÷ 3 = 44.7, then (44 + 50 + 54) ÷ 3 = 49.3, then (50 + 54 + 62) ÷ 3 = 55.3 thousand bags.

Measuring error. Compare each forecast with what actually sold. If the forecast was 66 thousand bags and 60 thousand sold, the error is 6 thousand, or 10% of actual sales. A method that is always too high is biased, which is worse than one that misses at random.

A decision. A new highway is announced near the dealer's town. The trend says 66,200 bags; building permits, a leading indicator, point higher. Plan the base order on the trend, and arrange with the supplier for a top-up if permits keep rising.

Links. Regression connects back to the demand function: its coefficients estimate how far each determinant moves sales.

text: The last chapter of the Arthaśāstra defines artha in terms of people's livelihood and the land they live on, and names the science as the means of acquiring and protecting that land. Livelihood, resources and the means to secure them sit close to the wealth, welfare and scarcity definitions above.
pairings.quote: मनुष्याणां वृत्तिरर्थः । manuṣyāṇāṃ vṛttir arthaḥ. “The livelihood of people is wealth.” Arthaśāstra 15.1.1

pairings.classic: the three-part test of kāma, artha, dharma
text: The tradition's four human aims include desire (kāma) and means (artha), bounded by right conduct (dharma). Desire alone does not make demand; it needs means, and the tradition adds a third test: whether the purchase is fitting. Willingness to pay, in modern terms, is that third part seen from the buyer's side.

Manu observes that desire is not quenched by consuming, as fire grows when fed with ghee. The Gītā says pleasures born of contact have a beginning and an end. The two lines sit on either side of the diminishing marginal utility debate: satisfaction per unit declines while the appetite persists.
pairings.quote: “Desire is never quenched by enjoyment of desires; it only grows, like fire fed with ghee.” न जातु कामः कामानामुपभोगेन शाम्यति । na jātu kāmaḥ kāmānām upabhogena śāmyati. Manusmṛti 2.94; Bhagavad Gītā 5.22

text: The Gītā's portrait of the over-proud mind includes boasting of wealth and birth: “who else is my equal?” That is the motive behind status buying. The same text notes that ordinary people follow whatever the eminent do, which describes imitation demand.
pairings.quote: आढ्योऽभिजनवानस्मि कोऽन्योऽस्ति सदृशो मया । āḍhyo 'bhijanavān asmi ko 'nyo 'sti sadṛśo mayā. Bhagavad Gītā 16.15; 3.21

text: The Arthaśāstra's Superintendent of Commerce fixes prices and permits a stated profit margin over cost, with a different margin for imported goods. Kauṭilya treats price as something a market officer sets and watches, which is a practical analogue to price determination.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.16; margins at 4.2

chapters.title: Elasticity of Demand
chapters.scope: How strongly quantity demanded responds to changes in price, income and the prices of related goods.

blocks.title: Measuring elasticity: PED, YED and XED
blocks.html:
A chai stall raises the price of a cup from ₹10 to ₹12. Will it take in more money, or less? That depends on how many customers walk away, and elasticity is the number that answers it.

In plain wordsElasticity measures how strongly buyers react to a change. It compares percentages, so it works the same for a ₹10 cup of tea and a ₹10 lakh car.

Exam definitionPrice elasticity of demand is the ratio of the percentage change in quantity demanded to the percentage change in price (Alfred Marshall).

If a small change brings a large change in quantity, demand is elastic. If a large change brings only a small change, it is inelastic. There are three measures, one for each kind of change.

MeasureFormulaReadingExample
PED, price elasticity% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price|PED| > 1 elastic, = 1 unitary, < 1 inelastic (sign ignored)Price up 10%, cups sold down 20%: PED = −2, elastic.
YED, income elasticity% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income> 1 luxury; between 0 and 1 necessity; 0 neutral; < 0 inferiorIncomes up 10%, restaurant meals up 15%: YED = 1.5, a luxury.
XED, cross elasticity% change in quantity of A ÷ % change in price of BPositive: substitutes. Negative: complements. Zero: unrelated.Coffee up 20%, tea sales up 10%: XED = +0.5, substitutes.

Back to the chai stall. At ₹10 it sells 200 cups a day and takes ₹2,000. At ₹12, a 20% rise, two things could happen:

  • Sales fall to 150 cups, a 25% fall. PED = −25 ÷ 20 = −1.25, elastic. Takings fall to ₹1,800.
  • Sales fall to 180 cups, a 10% fall. PED = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5, inelastic. Takings rise to ₹2,160.

Don't confuse elasticity with slope. Slope compares raw changes, such as cups per rupee. Elasticity compares percentages. Along a straight-line demand curve the slope is the same everywhere, but elasticity is high at high prices and low at low prices.

Elastic: buyers react more than the price moved. Inelastic: they react less.

blocks.title: Methods of measuring price elasticity
blocks.html:
Measure the same price change from two ends and you can get two different answers. The four methods below exist to settle which number to use.

1. Proportionate (percentage) method. It measures from the starting price and quantity.

e = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P) = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q)

It is simple, but the answer depends on the direction of the change. For the chai stall, ₹10 to ₹12 with sales falling from 200 to 150 gives −1.25. The reverse move, ₹12 to ₹10 with sales rising from 150 to 200, gives −2.

2. Point method. At a point on a straight-line demand curve, elasticity equals the lower segment ÷ upper segment of the line, measured from that point to the two axes. It is 1 at the midpoint, infinite where the line meets the price axis, and 0 where it meets the quantity axis. Use it when you have a demand line and want the elasticity at one price.

3. Arc (midpoint) method, for a stretch of the curve between two points:

e = [(Q₂ − Q₁) ÷ ((Q₁ + Q₂) ÷ 2)] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁) ÷ ((P₁ + P₂) ÷ 2)]

Averages make the answer the same in both directions. For the chai stall: (−50 ÷ 175) ÷ (2 ÷ 11) = −0.286 ÷ 0.182 = −1.57, whichever way the price moved.

4. Total outlay (expenditure) method, Alfred Marshall's: watch what happens to total spending, P × Q, when price changes. A kirana store sells 100 packets of biscuits a day at ₹20, taking ₹2,000. At ₹18 it sells 130 and takes ₹2,340. Spending rose as the price fell, so demand is elastic.

When price falls, total outlay…When price rises, total outlay…Elasticity
risesfallsGreater than 1 (elastic)
stays the samestays the sameEqual to 1 (unitary)
fallsrisesLess than 1 (inelastic)

Where it breaks. The total outlay method shows only whether demand is elastic, unitary or inelastic, not the exact value. The point method assumes a straight line, which real demand rarely is.

For exams. Expect an arc calculation with numbers, and the total outlay table as a reasoning question. A unitary demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, since spending stays the same at every price.

blocks.title: Five degrees of price elasticity
blocks.html:
Real goods sit between two extremes that almost never occur. Knowing the five reference points makes everything in between easy to place.

DegreePEDMeaningClosest real case
Perfectly elastic∞A tiny price rise cuts quantity demanded to zero. Horizontal curve.One farmer selling wheat at the going mandi price; a theoretical limit
Elastic> 1Quantity changes more than price. Flatter curve.One brand of biscuits among many
Unitary= 1Quantity changes in proportion to price; spending stays the same.A benchmark rather than a product
Inelastic< 1Quantity changes less than price. Steeper curve.Salt; petrol in the short run
Perfectly inelastic0Quantity does not change at any price. Vertical curve.A theoretical limit; life-saving medicine comes close

Don't read elasticity from steepness alone. Comparing two curves, flatter means more elastic only at the same price and quantity. Along one straight line, elasticity changes from point to point.

Flat is elastic. Steep is inelastic.

blocks.title: What makes demand elastic
blocks.html:
A rise in the price of salt barely changes how much people buy. A small discount on one phone brand can move its sales sharply. Five things explain the difference.

  • Substitutes: the more close substitutes, the more elastic the demand. One brand of tea has many; tea as a whole has few. So demand for a single brand is far more elastic than for the category.
  • Nature of the good: necessities are inelastic, luxuries elastic (salt and insulin against a foreign holiday).
  • Share of income: things that take a big share of a budget are more elastic than small purchases (a two-wheeler against a box of matches).
  • Time: demand grows more elastic over time, as people adjust. When petrol prices rise, people still commute next week; over some years, some switch to CNG, electric vehicles or the metro.
  • Durability: a durable purchase can be put off, so demand is more elastic (a refrigerator against bread).

Other factors: goods with many uses, such as electricity, have more elastic demand; purchases that can be postponed are more elastic than urgent ones such as medicines; habit makes demand inelastic, as with tobacco; and richer buyers react less to a given price change.

Where it breaks. The factors can pull in opposite directions. Petrol is a necessity with few substitutes in the short run, yet it takes a large share of a commuter's budget. Only data shows which wins.

blocks.title: Using elasticity in decisions
blocks.html:
A firm raises its price and sales fall. Was that a mistake? Elasticity turns the question into arithmetic.

Pricing. With elastic demand, a price cut raises revenue. With inelastic demand, a price rise raises revenue. For the chai stall that keeps 180 of its 200 customers at ₹12, the rise pays; if only 150 stay, it does not.

Taxation. Governments raise more revenue by taxing goods with inelastic demand, because sales fall little. That is one reason tobacco products in India are taxed at the highest GST rates.

Cross elasticity guides bundling of complements (a printer and its ink), analysis of competition from substitutes, and revenue forecasts when a competitor changes its price.
