For two perfect substitutes the cross elasticity tends to infinity. Income elasticity supports market segmentation and shows which products will grow as incomes rise.

Where it breaks. Elasticity is measured at one time, at one price, with other things held equal. Competitors may follow a price change, tastes shift, and a short-run elasticity can mislead a long-run decision.

In practice. Firms estimate elasticity from past promotions, price tests in a few markets, and surveys. Online sellers can test two prices on similar customers at the same time.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. You raised the price of a ₹200 product by 8%, and monthly volume fell 3%. Elasticity is about −0.375, so demand is inelastic, and revenue rose about 4.8% (1.08 × 0.97 = 1.048). Before raising the price again, ask whether competitors followed, and whether three months is long enough for buyers to have found alternatives.

Elasticity and margins. For a firm setting price to maximise profit, the margin over marginal cost, as a share of price, equals 1 ÷ |PED| (the Lerner rule). A firm facing an elasticity of −4 should price with a margin of about 25% of price; one facing −2, about 50%. The more elastic its demand, the thinner the margin it can hold.

Links. Pricing decisions (Unit 7) turns these numbers into pricing strategy. Market structures (this unit) explains why a firm in perfect competition faces a perfectly elastic demand curve.

chapters.lensNote: The classical texts have no measure of responsiveness. The links below are thematic: they concern necessities and the handling of scarcity, which is where elasticity matters in practice.

text: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad treats food as the base of life and tells the student not to disparage it, and to make it abundant. Food is the clearest inelastic good: demand barely moves when its price does. The text says nothing about prices or how buyers respond to them, so the link to elasticity is a reading.
pairings.quote: अन्नं न निन्द्यात् । तद्व्रतम् । annaṃ na nindyāt, tad vratam. “Do not disparage food; that is the vow.” Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.7; abundance at 3.9

text: When demand is inelastic, shortages produce steep price spikes. The Arthaśāstra shows a state that does not leave this to chance: it regulates traders' margins in the marketplace and prescribes relief measures for famine and other calamities. This is the practical case for price controls and buffer stocks that elasticity analysis supports today.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.16 and 4.2 (trade regulation); 4.3 (remedies against calamities)

chapters.title: Utility Analysis
chapters.scope: The cardinal approach: satisfaction can be measured in numbers called utils, and consumers allocate a budget to maximise total utility.

blocks.title: Core idea and assumptions
blocks.html: A consumer with a fixed budget spreads income across goods to get the most total utility. The cardinal approach assumes a rational consumer, utility that can be quantified in utils, goods that are divisible into small units, and diminishing marginal utility as consumption rises. It ignores ordinal ranking: it counts satisfaction, it does not compare bundles.

blocks.title: Total and marginal utility
blocks.html: Total utility (TU) is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed. Marginal utility (MU) is the additional satisfaction from one more unit. As consumption rises, MU falls.

blocks.title: Law of diminishing marginal utility
blocks.html:
As a person consumes more of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit decreases, other things remaining constant.

UnitsMUTUWhat to notice
11212MU is continuously falling
2820TU rises while MU is positive
3525TU rises at a diminishing rate
4328
5028TU is maximum when MU = 0
6−226TU falls when MU turns negative

blocks.title: Law of equi-marginal utility
blocks.html:
MU₁ ÷ P₁ = MU₂ ÷ P₂ = MU₃ ÷ P₃

A consumer maximises total utility when the marginal utility per rupee is equal across all goods. If MU per rupee is higher for good A, shift spending to A until the ratios level out. This is consumer equilibrium in the cardinal approach: no further reallocation raises total utility.

blocks.title: Consumer surplus
blocks.html:
Consumer surplus = total utility in money − total expenditure

It is the gap between what a buyer is willing to pay and what is paid. If willingness to pay is ₹1,500 and the price paid is ₹1,200, surplus is ₹300. If the price rises to ₹1,300, surplus falls to ₹200.

text: The Gītā says that contacts with the senses bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and that they come and go. Utility from one unit is not a fixed quantity, which is why measuring it in utils is an assumption and not a fact.
pairings.quote: आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास् । āgamāpāyino 'nityās. “They come and go, and are impermanent.” Bhagavad Gītā 2.14

text: Manu's line about desire growing under consumption (see chapter 6) and the Gītā's line that contact-born pleasures have a beginning and an end together describe the two halves of the consumer: appetite remains while the satisfaction per unit declines.
pairings.quote: “Pleasures born of contact are sources of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, and the wise take no delight in them.” ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते । आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः । ye hi saṃsparśajā bhogā duḥkhayonaya eva te, ādyantavantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ. Manusmṛti 2.94; Bhagavad Gītā 5.22

text: The Gītā says yoga is not for one who eats too much or too little, sleeps too much or too little. It prescribes balance across food, recreation, work and sleep. This is equi-marginal logic applied to a day: shift effort from where it adds little to where it adds more.
pairings.quote: नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः । nātyaśnatas tu yogo 'sti na caikāntam anaśnataḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 6.16–17

text: Consumer surplus measures the value received above the price paid. The Yoga Sūtras name contentment (santoṣa) as a source of the highest happiness, and the Īśa Upaniṣad advises enjoying what one has without coveting another's wealth. Both locate satisfaction in what is received, not in the price.
pairings.quote: सन्तोषादनुत्तमः सुखलाभः । santoṣād anuttamaḥ sukhalābhaḥ. Yoga Sūtra 2.42; Īśa Upaniṣad 1

chapters.title: Indifference Curve Analysis
chapters.scope: The ordinal approach: utility is ranked, not measured. Consumers compare bundles and choose the one they prefer within their budget.

blocks.title: The ordinal approach
blocks.html: The ordinal approach drops utils. It asks only whether a consumer prefers bundle A to bundle B, and it uses two tools, the indifference curve and the budget constraint, to find the choice. Its assumptions: a rational consumer who prefers more to less; complete preferences (every bundle can be ranked); transitivity (if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C); divisible goods; non-satiation (more is preferred); and no cardinal measurement of utility.

blocks.title: Indifference curve
blocks.html:
An indifference curve (IC) shows all combinations of two goods that give the same satisfaction. Its properties:

  • Downward sloping: more of X requires less of Y to keep satisfaction the same.
  • Convex to the origin: reflects a diminishing marginal rate of substitution.
  • Never intersect: each IC represents one distinct level of utility.
  • Higher IC, higher utility: curves farther from the origin are preferred.

blocks.title: Marginal rate of substitution (MRS)
blocks.html: MRS is the rate at which a consumer will give up one good to gain one more unit of another, holding satisfaction constant. As the consumer has more of X and less of Y, willingness to give up Y falls, so MRS diminishes and the curve becomes convex.

blocks.title: Budget line
blocks.html: The budget line shows every bundle of two goods the consumer can buy with a given income at given prices. Conditions: income fixed, prices constant, entire income spent, two goods considered. Its slope is −Px/Py, the opportunity cost of one good in units of the other. Bundles on or inside the line are affordable; those outside are not.

blocks.title: Consumer equilibrium
blocks.html:
The consumer reaches the highest affordable IC where the IC touches the budget line. At this point of tangency, MRS = Px/Py, so the slope of the IC equals the slope of the budget line.

BasisCardinal approachOrdinal approach
MeasurementUtility measured in utilsUtility ranked; no numerical measure
ToolsTU and MUIndifference curves and MRS
EquilibriumMU per rupee equalisedMRS = price ratio (Px/Py)
FocusAbsolute satisfactionRelative preference
PracticalityMeasurement is difficultMore practical, widely used

Memory cue: cardinal asks how much? Ordinal asks which is preferred?

text: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad sets out a ranking, not a measurement: the good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both present themselves, and the wise person examines them and chooses. It is a classical statement of ordinal choice, where the question is which option is preferred.
pairings.quote: श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतस्तौ सम्परीत्य विविनक्ति धीरः । śreyaś ca preyaś ca manuṣyam etas tau samparītya vivinakti dhīraḥ. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.2

text: Kauṭilya says to enjoy pleasures without breaking the claims of right conduct and wealth, or to pursue the three aims in balance, each supporting the others. This is an allocation across competing goods under a constraint, with the constraint stated in moral terms.
pairings.quote: धर्मार्थाविरोधेन कामं सेवेत । dharmārthāvirodhena kāmaṃ seveta. Arthaśāstra 1.7.3

text: The Gītā advises treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike (sukha-duḥkhe same kṛtvā). Indifference between bundles is not that teaching, and the resemblance is in the word only. The text is about steadiness of mind under outcomes, not about equal-satisfaction trade-offs.
pairings.quote: “Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike.” सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ । sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau. Bhagavad Gītā 2.38; 2.48

chapters.title: Market Structures
chapters.scope: How markets are classified by the number of sellers, the product and ease of entry, and how that fixes price and profit.

blocks.title: What a market is
blocks.html:
In economics a market is not a place but the whole set of buyers and sellers of a commodity in contact with each other. Cournot described it as the whole of any region in which buyers and sellers are in such free contact that the prices of the same goods tend to equality easily and quickly. A market needs buyers and sellers, a commodity, contact between them through bargaining or exchange, knowledge of conditions, and tends toward one price at a given time.

What determines a market's structure: the number and size of sellers and of buyers, the nature of the product (homogeneous or differentiated), the conditions of entry and exit, and economies of scale.

StructureBuyersExample
MonopsonyOne buyerA single large employer of labour in a town
DuopsonyTwo buyersTwo mills buying a region's crop
OligopsonyA few buyersSugarcane growers selling to a few local sugar mills
Bilateral monopolyOne seller facing one buyerA single union bargaining with a single employer; price is settled by bargaining within limits

blocks.title: Revenue: total, average and marginal
blocks.html:
TR = P × Q   ·   AR = TR ÷ Q = P   ·   MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ = TRn − TRn−1

Because average revenue equals price, the AR curve is the firm's demand curve.

  • Perfect competition: the firm sells any quantity at the market price, so AR = MR = P, both horizontal, and TR is a straight line from the origin.
  • Imperfect competition: to sell one more unit the firm must lower the price on all units, so MR is below AR. For a straight-line AR, MR falls twice as steeply and cuts the quantity axis halfway to where AR meets it.
  • MR can be negative. TR is at its maximum where MR = 0.

Revenue and elasticity are linked:

MR = AR × (1 − 1 ÷ e)

So MR is positive where demand is elastic (e > 1), zero where it is unitary (e = 1), and negative where it is inelastic (e < 1).

blocks.title: The four market structures
blocks.html:
FeaturePerfect competitionMonopolistic competitionOligopolyMonopoly
SellersVery manyManyFewOne
ProductHomogeneousDifferentiatedHomogeneous or differentiatedUnique, no close substitute
EntryFreeRelatively easyDifficultBlocked
Price controlNone (price taker)LimitedConsiderableHigh (price maker)
Demand curveHorizontalDownward slopingKinked, indeterminateDownward sloping
RevenueAR = MR = PAR > MRMR has a gapAR > MR
Non-price competitionNoneSignificant (advertising)Very strongLittle (mainly informative advertising)
Long-run profitNormalNormalSupernormal possibleSupernormal possible
ExamplesWheat, riceRestaurants, clothing, cosmeticsAutomobiles, airlines, steel, cementLocal electricity board, patented drugs

Normal profit is the minimum return needed to keep a firm in an industry. Supernormal profit is any return above it.

blocks.title: Perfect competition
blocks.html:
Under perfect competition every firm is a price taker: the industry sets the price through demand and supply, and each firm faces a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve at that price.

Conditions: a large number of buyers and sellers; a homogeneous product; free entry and exit; perfect knowledge; perfect mobility of factors; and no transport or selling costs. Edward Chamberlin called the first three, many sellers, a homogeneous product and free entry, pure competition; perfect competition adds the rest.

PeriodSupplyPrice set by
Market period (very short run)Fixed: perfectly inelastic for perishables such as fish; for durable goods, sellers hold back stock below a reserve priceDemand
Short runVaries with output from existing plantDemand and supply
Long runPlant size can change and firms enter or leaveMainly cost

Equilibrium. The firm produces where MR = MC, with MC rising, and since MR = P this means P = MC. In the short run it may earn supernormal profit, normal profit or a loss; it shuts down if price falls below average variable cost. In the long run, entry and exit remove supernormal profit and losses, so P = AR = MR = MC = minimum average cost, and every firm earns normal profit.

blocks.title: Monopoly and monopolistic competition
blocks.html:
A monopoly is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry: patents, licences and franchises, control of a key input, or economies of scale large enough to make one firm the cheapest supplier (a natural monopoly). The firm is the industry.

Monopoly equilibrium: output where MR = MC, with MC cutting MR from below; price read off the demand (AR) curve above. A monopolist can set the price or the quantity, not both. Because MR is positive only where demand is elastic, a profit-maximising monopolist always produces on the elastic part of its demand curve. Supernormal profit can last into the long run, since entry is blocked, though short-run losses are possible.

Monopolistic competition was set out by Edward Chamberlin in The Theory of Monopolistic Competition (1933); Joan Robinson's The Economics of Imperfect Competition appeared the same year. Its features: many sellers; product differentiation by brand, quality, design and packaging; close but not perfect substitutes; free entry and exit; heavy selling costs and non-price competition; and a product group rather than an industry. Each firm has a monopoly over its own brand only, which gives it limited control over price. Examples: soaps, toothpaste, restaurants, clothing.

Equilibrium: in the short run, MR = MC, with supernormal profit possible. In the long run, new entrants draw buyers away until the demand curve is just tangent to the average cost curve on its falling part: price equals average cost, profit is normal, and each firm works below its lowest-cost output, leaving excess capacity.

blocks.title: Oligopoly and duopoly
blocks.html:
An oligopoly has a few sellers, each large enough that its decisions affect the others. Its marks are interdependence, barriers to entry, heavy advertising, and a demand curve that cannot be known without guessing rivals' reactions. A pure oligopoly sells a homogeneous product (steel, cement, aluminium); a differentiated oligopoly sells branded products (cars, televisions). Each firm is torn between two motives: to act alone and maximise its own profit, or to cooperate with rivals and maximise their joint profit. A duopoly is an oligopoly of two sellers.

ModelAssumptionResult
Cournot (1838)Two firms each choose output, taking the rival's output as givenEach produces one-third of the competitive output; two-thirds in total
Bertrand (1883)Firms compete on price for an identical productPrice is driven down to marginal cost
Edgeworth (1897)Price competition with limited capacityPrice oscillates with no stable equilibrium
Stackelberg (1934)One firm leads in setting output; the other followsThe leader gains a larger share
Kinked demand: Paul Sweezy, and R. L. Hall and C. J. Hitch (1939)Rivals match a price cut but ignore a price risePrices stay rigid; the model explains stability but not how the price was first set

Collusion. Firms may cooperate openly through a cartel, which fixes a joint price and allots output quotas, such as OPEC; or tacitly through price leadership, where others follow a low-cost, dominant or barometric firm's price.

blocks.title: Price determination
blocks.html:
Every profit-maximising firm in every structure sets output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR). What differs is the price it can charge at that output.

  • Perfect competition: the firm cannot influence price, so P = MR, and it equals MC at equilibrium. Price taker.
  • Monopolistic competition: P > MR, so the firm has partial price control, with product differentiation and heavy advertising.
  • Oligopoly: firms are interdependent. The kinked demand curve says rivals match a price cut but ignore a price rise, so demand is flat above the prevailing price and steep below it. The kink leaves a gap in the MR curve, which explains price rigidity.
  • Monopoly: P > MR, with full control over price, and supernormal profit can persist because entry is blocked.

blocks.title: Price discrimination, dumping and reverse dumping
blocks.html: Price discrimination is charging different prices for the same product to different buyers or markets when the difference is not due to cost. It needs three conditions: the seller has monopoly power, the markets can be separated with resale prevented, and elasticity differs across markets. The degrees are A. C. Pigou's (The Economics of Welfare, 1920): first (perfect) charges each buyer their individual willingness to pay, taking all consumer surplus; second prices by quantity or blocks; third divides buyers into market segments. In third-degree discrimination the firm sets MR equal in every market and to MC, charging the higher price where demand is less elastic; if elasticities were equal, discrimination would not pay. Electricity charged at different rates to domestic, commercial and industrial users is a common example. Dumping is selling a good abroad at a lower price than at home, or below its cost, to win a foreign market. Reverse dumping is international price discrimination in which a firm sells abroad at a higher price than at home.

text: The Arthaśāstra, in its chapter on the control of traders, names the problem of merchants who combine to hold back goods and fix prices for gain, and prescribes penalties. This is cartel behaviour, the oligopolist's temptation, and an early case for competition policy.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 4.2 (control of traders)

text: The Superintendent of Commerce permits a different profit margin on local goods and on foreign goods. It is regulated differential pricing by market. The state, not the seller, sets the difference, and the reason given is protection of the buyer, not extraction of surplus.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.16; margins at 4.2

pairings.modern: Monopoly power exercised by the state
text: Book 2 describes enterprises such as mines and the manufacture of certain goods placed under state superintendents. These are public monopolies in the modern sense, run with accountability for revenue and quality.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra, Book 2 (superintendents of mines and manufactures)

chapters.title: National Income and Inflation
chapters.scope: How an economy's output and income are measured, and what happens when the general price level keeps rising.

blocks.title: National income
blocks.html:
National income is the monetary value of all final goods and services produced in an economy over a year, measured at factor cost. Counting only final output avoids double counting. Three methods measure it, and in principle all give the same answer: output (value added) = income = expenditure.

  • Product or value-added method: the value of output minus intermediate consumption, summed over every stage of production.
  • Income method: NI = W + R + I + P (wages, rent, interest, profit).
  • Expenditure method: C + I + G + (X − M).

blocks.title: Concepts and formulas
blocks.html:
ConceptMeaningFormula
GDPMarket value of final goods and services produced within domestic bordersC + I + G + (X − M): consumption, investment, government expenditure, exports minus imports
GNPIncome earned by a country's residents at home and abroadGDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA)
NNPGNP after allowing for depreciationGNP − depreciation
National incomeFactor income at factor costNNP at market price − indirect taxes + subsidies
Personal incomeIncome actually received by individuals before direct taxesNI − undistributed profits − corporate taxes + transfers
Disposable incomeIncome left after personal taxesPI − personal taxes
Per capita incomeAverage income per person; a standard-of-living indicatorNI ÷ population

The flow runs GDP → GNP → NNP → national income → personal income → disposable income.

blocks.title: Inflation
blocks.html:
Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level, which lowers purchasing power. Three causes: demand-pull (aggregate demand exceeds what the economy can supply, so prices rise), cost-push (production costs rise and are passed on) and built-in (a wage-price spiral driven by expectations of future inflation).

TermMeaning
Walking inflationModerate, roughly 3–10%; erodes purchasing power gradually
Running inflationRapid, roughly 10–20%; signals an overheating economy
HyperinflationExtreme and uncontrolled, above 50% a month; usually ends in currency collapse
DisinflationThe inflation rate slows; prices still rise, but more slowly
DeflationThe price level falls
StagflationHigh inflation together with high unemployment and stagnant growth

blocks.title: Measuring inflation
blocks.html:
CPI = current basket price ÷ base price × 100 · WPI = current wholesale price ÷ base price × 100 · GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100

CPI tracks consumer-level prices and the cost of living. WPI tracks bulk and producer prices and excludes services. The GDP deflator covers every good and service in the economy and uses a changing basket.

blocks.title: Effects and control
blocks.html:
Moderate inflation can lift spending, investment, production and employment. High inflation cuts purchasing power and savings, deepens inequality and raises uncertainty. Four sets of tools are used to control it:

  • Monetary policy: central bank raises interest rates and reserve ratios, uses open market operations.
  • Fiscal policy: government lowers spending and raises taxes.
  • Price control measures: price ceilings, subsidies, rationing.
  • Supply-side measures: raise production, remove supply bottlenecks, improve efficiency and logistics.

text: The Arthaśāstra lists the heads of the state's revenue: fortified cities, countryside, mines, irrigation works, forests, herds and trade routes. It pairs them with an accounts office that records income and expenditure. It is an early sectoral accounting of an economy.
pairings.quote: समाहर्ता दुर्गं राष्ट्रं खनिं सेतुं वनं व्रजं वणिक्पथं चावेक्षेत । samāhartā durgaṃ rāṣṭraṃ khaniṃ setuṃ vanaṃ vrajaṃ vaṇikpathaṃ cāvekṣeta. Arthaśāstra 2.6.1; accounts office at 2.7

text: Manu advises taking tax in small amounts, as a leech, a calf and a bee take their food. Kālidāsa describes a king who takes tax as the sun takes water, to return it many times over. Taxation is tied to a limit and to a return for the public.
pairings.quote: “As the bee takes honey little by little, so the king should draw taxes.” यथाल्पाल्पमदन्त्याद्यं वार्योकोवत्सषट्पदाः । yathālpālpam adanty ādyaṃ vāryokovatsaṣaṭpadāḥ. Manusmṛti 7.129; Raghuvaṃśa 1.18

text: Where price ceilings, rationing and stock management appear in modern inflation policy, the Arthaśāstra describes the superintendent of commerce fixing prices and prescribes relief measures in calamity. It also provides for official regulation of the mint. The state is expected to act on prices directly when markets fail.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.16; 4.2; 4.3; the mint at 2.12

chapters.title: Business Ethics and CSR
chapters.scope: Moral principles applied to commercial decisions, and a firm's responsibility to the society it operates in.

blocks.title: Ethics, morals and values
blocks.html:
A kirana owner finds that his wholesaler has billed him ₹2,000 too little. Nobody will notice if he stays quiet. What he does next draws on three different things: ethics, morals and values.

In plain wordsBusiness ethics is working out what is right, not only what is profitable or legal, when you run or work in a business.

Exam definitionBusiness ethics is the study of business situations, activities and decisions where issues of right and wrong are addressed (Crane and Matten).

The three words are often used as if they meant the same thing. They do not.

TermMeaningIn the kirana example
EthicsStandards and codes that guide right behaviourThe traders' shared rule: bill honestly, and correct errors either way
MoralsPersonal beliefs about right and wrongHis own sense that keeping the money would be a kind of stealing
ValuesDeeply held principles about what is importantHe cares more about being known as honest than about ₹2,000

Business ethics applies moral principles to business decisions, balancing profit with social welfare. It does three things for a firm:

  • Builds trust and reputation. A wholesaler who is told about the error has a reason to trust this shop with credit next time.
  • Promotes fairness and accountability. People know the rules, and know they will answer for breaking them.
  • Supports long-term sustainability. A shortcut that pays this month can cost customers, staff and licences later.

Don't confuse ethics with law. Law is the minimum that society enforces. Ethics asks what is right, including where the law is silent or out of date. Some acts are legal but unethical, such as hiding a known product defect that no rule yet covers. Keeping the wholesaler's ₹2,000 may never reach a court, but it is still wrong.

Where it breaks. A firm can print an ethics code and still reward the staff who cut corners. People also hold different values, so "right" is often argued over rather than looked up. Ethics gives the questions; it does not settle every case by itself.

For exams. Expect a matching question on the three terms: ethics are codes, morals are personal beliefs, values are what a person holds important. Remember the phrase "balancing profit with social welfare".

Ethics are codes, morals are beliefs, values are what matters.

blocks.title: Principles of business ethics
blocks.html:
A sales team must hit its Diwali target. A discount only for friends, a quiet word with a rival about prices, a hidden charge on the bill: each would help. The principles of business ethics are the checklist that rules them out.

There are eight principles. Each one names a standard and, by implication, a typical way of breaking it. The breaches below are illustrations.

PrincipleWhat it asksA breach looks like
ImpartialityFairness and equalityGiving a contract to a relative without comparing bids
Legal complianceObey the laws and regulationsSkipping a safety inspection to save a day
AccountabilityTake responsibility, with transparencyBlaming a junior for a decision the manager made
Trust and honestyTell the truth and keep promisesSelling a refurbished phone as new
Fair practicesEthical pricing and competition; no corruptionFixing prices with a rival; paying a bribe for a licence
Due diligenceAssess risks and consequences before actingSigning a supplier without checking how it treats workers
Social obligationBenefit society, not only the firmLetting a plant's waste run into a village stream
Stakeholder interestWeigh employees, customers, investors and the communityClosing a factory without warning its workers or the town

How to use them. Run a decision past all eight before you act. Take the Diwali target. A friends-only discount fails impartiality. Agreeing prices with a rival fails fair practices, and may also fail legal compliance. A hidden charge fails trust and honesty. A plain store-wide offer passes all eight.

Don't confuse principles with a code of conduct. Principles are general standards that apply to any firm. A code of conduct is one firm's written rules that apply them to its own situations, such as how large a gift staff may accept.

Where it breaks. The principles can pull against each other. Stakeholder interest may call for keeping a loss-making plant open; duty to investors may call for closing it. The list tells you what to weigh, not how to weigh it. The decision approaches in this chapter help with that.

For exams. Learn the eight by name and match each to its meaning. "Assessing risks and consequences" is due diligence. "Ethical pricing, competition and anti-corruption" is fair practices. The four stakeholder groups named are employees, customers, investors and the community.

blocks.title: Ethical issue and ethical dilemma
blocks.html:
Sales at an auto-parts plant in Pune have fallen by a third. The owner can lay off 200 of its 1,000 workers, or keep them all and risk the whole firm failing. Neither choice is clean.

In plain wordsAn ethical issue is a wrong you should simply not do. An ethical dilemma is a choice where every option costs something you rightly value.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: an ethical dilemma is a situation in which a person must choose between two or more options, each backed by a moral value or obligation, so that no option satisfies them all.

FeatureEthical issueEthical dilemma
What it isA business action that violates moral principlesA choice between conflicting moral values or obligations
The questionIs this wrong?Which right comes first?
ExamplesData falsification, insider trading, labour exploitationLayoffs against avoiding bankruptcy
What it needsThe will to refuse, and controls that catch itCareful reasoning about who gains and who loses

Three checks help to frame any hard case:

  1. Who is affected? In Pune: the 200 workers and their families, the 800 who stay, lenders, suppliers and customers.
  2. Which values conflict? Loyalty to long-serving workers against the duty to keep the firm alive for everyone else.
  3. What is legal is not always ethical. A layoff may follow every rule and still be handled unfairly. How much notice, what support, and who is rehired first are ethical choices too.

Don't confuse a dilemma with a temptation. Falsifying data to meet a target can feel like a hard choice. But only one side is a moral value; the other is self-interest. That makes it an ethical issue. Rushworth Kidder called real dilemmas "right versus right" choices, and temptations "right versus wrong".

Where it breaks. The three checks set out the problem; they do not solve it. Two careful people can run the same checks and still disagree, because they weigh the values differently. The decision approaches in the next section give them ways to reason it through.

In practice. Kenneth Blanchard and Norman Vincent Peale offered three quick questions: Is it legal? Is it balanced, or fair to all concerned? How will it make me feel about myself? A plan that fails any one deserves a second look.

For exams. Expect to classify examples. Insider trading, bribery and falsified accounts are issues. Choices such as layoffs against closure, or a client's confidentiality against public safety, are dilemmas.

An issue breaks a principle; a dilemma sets two values against each other.

blocks.title: Decision approaches and theories
blocks.html:
A drug company can price a new medicine high, to fund the next round of research, or low, so poor patients can afford it. Thoughtful people reach different answers because they ask different questions.

In plain wordsAn ethical theory is a test of what makes an action right: its results, the duty it follows, or the character it shows.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: teleological theories judge an action by its consequences; deontological theories judge it by duty or principle, regardless of outcome.

Five approaches to a decision. Each asks one question. The last column applies it to the medicine.

ApproachQuestion it asksApplied to the medicine
UtilitarianWhich action gives the greatest good to the greatest number?Which price helps most people overall, counting future patients that research may help?
RightsDoes it protect individual rights and freedoms?Does a high price deny patients a right to treatment?
JusticeIs treatment fair and equitable?Are rich and poor patients treated fairly, for example by charging them different prices?
Common goodDoes it serve community welfare and shared benefits?Does the choice support a health system everyone depends on?
Virtue ethicsWhat would a person of honesty, courage and compassion do?What would an honest and compassionate firm do here?

At the level of theory, the families are:

  • Teleological ethics judges by consequences: ethical egoism (my own long-term good), utilitarianism (everyone's good, counted equally) and eudaimonism (human flourishing).
  • Deontological ethics judges by duty and principle, regardless of outcome: rights theory, social contract and social justice.
  • Virtue ethics looks at the decision-maker's moral character: prudence, courage, integrity and responsibility.
  • Meta-ethics asks about the nature and meaning of ethical principles, such as what "good" means.
  • Applied ethics addresses concrete problems in business, medicine and the environment.

Don't confuse utilitarianism with ethical egoism. Both judge by consequences. Egoism counts only the decision-maker's good; utilitarianism counts everyone's good equally. Also keep meta-ethics (what ethical words mean) apart from applied ethics (what to do in a real case).

Where it breaks. Utilitarianism can justify harming a few for the gain of many. Deontology struggles when two duties clash. Virtue ethics describes a good person but gives little guidance on a specific choice. That is why careful decision-makers test a choice against several approaches, not one.

For exams. Expect to classify: utilitarianism and egoism are teleological; rights, social contract and social justice are deontological. Match "greatest good of the greatest number" to the utilitarian approach.

Go deeper for practitioners

The thinkers behind the labels. Utilitarianism comes from Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. Immanuel Kant is the central deontologist: act only on a rule you could want everyone to follow, and never treat people merely as a means. Virtue ethics goes back to Aristotle. John Rawls's justice theory asks which rules you would choose behind a "veil of ignorance", not knowing what position you would hold.

A decision. Your firm can save ₹50 lakh a year by moving work to a supplier that pays below the local norm. A utilitarian test looks at total gains and losses. A rights test asks whether the workers are being exploited. A virtue test asks whether you would defend the choice in front of your own staff. When the tests disagree, write down why you chose the one you followed.

blocks.title: Corporate social responsibility
blocks.html:
A cement plant earns well from its site near a village. Dust settles on the fields, and the village school has no toilets. Whether the company should act, and how far, is the question of corporate social responsibility.

In plain wordsCSR is a company taking responsibility for its effect on people and the planet, not only on its profits.

Exam definitionThe social responsibility of business encompasses the economic, legal, ethical and discretionary expectations that society has of organisations at a given point in time (Archie Carroll, 1979).

CSR integrates social, environmental and economic responsibility into business operations. It aims at shared value, where business success and social welfare reinforce each other. Its outcomes include a better corporate image, investor attraction, employee morale, compliance and sustainable development.

CSR in India. India moved from guidelines to law in four steps.

YearCSR in India
2009CSR guidelines introduced
2011National Voluntary Guidelines, nine principles
2013CSR provisions introduced in company law
2014CSR rules came into force on 1 April 2014, making India the first country to make CSR spending mandatory

Applicability: a company that meets any one of these thresholds: net worth of ₹500 crore or more, turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more. Spend: at least 2% of the average net profit of the preceding three years. Focus areas include education, the environment and rural development.

Worked example (illustrative). Company A has a net worth of ₹300 crore, turnover of ₹800 crore and net profit of ₹7 crore.

  1. Net worth and turnover are below their thresholds. Net profit, ₹7 crore, is above ₹5 crore. One test is enough, so the law applies.
  2. Its net profits for the preceding three years were ₹5 crore, ₹6 crore and ₹7 crore. Average: (5 + 6 + 7) ÷ 3 = ₹6 crore.
  3. Minimum spend: 2% of ₹6 crore = ₹0.12 crore = ₹12 lakh.

Company B, with a net worth of ₹450 crore, turnover of ₹900 crore and net profit of ₹4 crore, meets none of the three tests and is not covered.

Don't confuse CSR with charity. Charity is only the top layer of Carroll's pyramid. CSR starts with how the money is earned: fair pay, safe products and clean production. A firm that pollutes a river and funds a school nearby has not met its responsibility.

Where it breaks. Milton Friedman argued in 1970 that the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits, within the rules. Others warn that CSR can become box-ticking: a law that sets a spend measures money paid out, not good done.

For exams. Learn the three thresholds (any one is enough), the 2% of three years' average net profit, the years 2009, 2011, 2013 and 2014, and Carroll's four layers in order.

Go deeper for practitioners

Shared value. Michael Porter and Mark Kramer (2011) argued that firms should look for "shared value": business opportunities in social problems, such as a dairy that trains its farmers and so gets better milk. They presented it as different from CSR spent as an add-on.

The triple bottom line. John Elkington proposed that firms report on people and the planet as well as profit. Many sustainability reports follow that idea.

A decision. Company A's ₹12 lakh could fund a one-day health camp in a city, or toilets for the school beside its own plant. The camp gets more press. The toilets answer a need the plant's neighbours actually have, and build trust where the firm operates. Which would you defend to the village, and to your board?

text: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad's farewell instruction to students turns on conduct: speak the truth, follow right conduct, and do only blameless actions. It then gives a method for giving, which is relevant to CSR: give with faith, in abundance, with modesty, and with a sense of responsibility.
pairings.quote: सत्यं वद । धर्मं चर । satyaṃ vada, dharmaṃ cara. “Speak the truth; practise right conduct.” श्रद्धया देयम् । श्रिया देयम् । ह्रिया देयम् । śraddhayā deyam, śriyā deyam, hriyā deyam. Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1–3

text: A Ṛgvedic hymn says the one who eats alone eats sin alone. The Gītā adds that those who cook only for themselves eat sin, and that one should act with an eye to the welfare of the world. The pairing speaks to the tension at the centre of business ethics.
pairings.quote: केवलाघो भवति केवलादी । kevalāgho bhavati kevalādī. “He who eats alone eats only sin.” Ṛgveda 10.117.6; Bhagavad Gītā 3.13, 3.20

pairings.classic: delight in the welfare of all beings
text: The Gītā describes those who are devoted to the welfare of all beings as reaching the supreme. The phrase is an old statement of the stakeholder view.
pairings.quote: सर्वभूतहिते रताः । sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 5.25; 12.4

text: The Gītā lists the qualities of a person oriented to the good: fearlessness, purity of heart, charity, self-control, straightforwardness, non-violence, truthfulness and others. This is a virtue list, and it is paired with a list of opposing vices.
pairings.quote: अभयं सत्त्वसंशुद्धिर्ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थितिः । दानं दमश्च … abhayaṃ sattvasaṃśuddhir jñānayogavyavasthitiḥ, dānaṃ damaś ca… Bhagavad Gītā 16.1–3

text: The Gītā begins with a dilemma. Arjuna says his mind is confused about duty and asks to be taught. Later the text admits that the course of action is hard to understand. It does not claim that dilemmas are easy.
pairings.quote: धर्मसम्मूढचेताः । dharmasammūḍhacetāḥ. “My mind confused about duty.” गहना कर्मणो गतिः । gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ. “The way of action is deep.” Bhagavad Gītā 2.7; 4.17

text: Modern theory sets deontology, teleology and virtue against each other. The Gītā can be read as holding all three: act from duty (svadharma), stay even-minded about results, and aim at the welfare of all, from a trained character. It is a synthesis offered for reflection, since the Gītā does not use these categories.

pairings.classic: earn by labour, give with your own hand
text: Guru Nanak's salok names two marks of someone who knows the way: they live on what they earn by their own work, and they give part of it away with their own hands. CSR asks a company to earn fairly and to share part of its profit with society. The salok is about a person, not a firm, so the parallel is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Those who eat what they earn by their labour, and give some of it from their own hands: Nanak, they know the way.” ਘਾਲਿ ਖਾਇ ਕਿਛੁ ਹਥਹੁ ਦੇਇ ॥ ਨਾਨਕ ਰਾਹੁ ਪਛਾਣਹਿ ਸੇਇ ॥ ghāli khāi kichhu hathahu dei, nānak rāhu pachhāṇahi sei. Guru Granth Sahib, p. 1245 (Guru Nānak, salok in Rāg Sāraṅg)

chapters.title: Corporate Governance and Value-Based Organisations
chapters.scope: How a company is directed and controlled, and what changes when values, not only profit, shape its culture and strategy.

blocks.title: Corporate governance
blocks.html:
Lakhs of small shareholders own a listed company, but a few managers run it. The owners cannot watch every decision. Something must keep the managers working for the company rather than for themselves.

In plain wordsCorporate governance is the set of rules and checks that decide who controls a company and how they are held to account.

Exam definitionCorporate governance is the system by which companies are directed and controlled (Cadbury Report, 1992).

A fuller version: corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled so that stakeholder interests are balanced.

Two theories start from opposite views of the manager.

TheoryView of the managerWhat governance should do
Agency theoryManagers (agents) may act in their own interest against the shareholders (principals). The conflict is managed through audits and performance incentives.Monitor and align: independent directors, audits, pay linked to performance, full disclosure
Stewardship theoryManagers are trustworthy stewards of the company, not self-interested agents.Empower: give managers authority and support, and avoid controls that signal distrust

An illustration. A CEO's bonus depends only on this year's profit. She can lift profit by ₹5 crore by putting off machine maintenance, though the delay will cost ₹15 crore in repairs later. Agency theory predicts that some managers will make that trade. Linking pay to performance over several years, and an audit committee that asks about maintenance, make it less attractive.

The OECD Principles of Corporate Governance, first issued in 1999, are international guidelines. They cover shareholder rights, equitable treatment of shareholders, transparency and disclosure, the role of stakeholders, and the responsibilities of the board.

Don't confuse governance with management. Management runs the business day to day. Governance decides who directs the managers, and checks that they serve the company. Also keep the roles straight: shareholders are the principals; managers are the agents.

Where it breaks. Heavy monitoring costs money, and good managers may read it as distrust. Pure stewardship can be naive when pay and power invite abuse. In many Indian companies a promoter family holds control, so the sharper conflict is often between controlling and minority shareholders, not between owners and hired managers.

For exams. Know the Cadbury definition, which party is the principal and which the agent, how agency theory differs from stewardship theory, and the areas the OECD Principles cover.

Go deeper for practitioners

Agency costs. Michael Jensen and William Meckling (1976) named the costs of the owner–manager split. They include the cost of monitoring managers, and the value lost when managers still act for themselves.

In India. The Companies Act, 2013 requires independent directors and audit committees for specified classes of companies. Listed companies must also follow SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations, 2015, which replaced Clause 49 of the listing agreement.

A case. In January 2009, the chairman of Satyam Computer Services admitted that the company's accounts had been falsified for years. The board, the auditors and the investors had all relied on figures that were not true. If you sat on a board today, what would you ask for, beyond the audited accounts, to be sure the cash really exists?

blocks.title: Value-based organisation (VBO)
blocks.html:
Two firms have the same written rule on gifts from suppliers. In one, staff quietly accept them. In the other, they hand them back without being asked. The rulebook is the same; the shared values are not.

In plain wordsA value-based organisation is one where shared values, not only rules and targets, decide how people behave.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a VBO is an organisation in which ethical values shape culture, leadership and strategy, and societal contribution ranks alongside profit.

Its main features:

  • Values first. Ethical values shape culture, leadership and strategy.
  • Profit with purpose. Contribution to society ranks alongside profit, not after it.
  • Vision at the top. The vision statement, the long-term aspirational direction, sits at the top of its hierarchy.
  • Trust as the core success factor, built through consistent ethical conduct and shared values.

An illustration. An auto-parts firm in Pune states its vision as "safe vehicles for every Indian family". One core value follows: safety before schedule. In practice, any line worker may stop the line on finding a defect, and is thanked for it, even when an order is late. The vision is now visible in a daily decision.

Why trust matters. When staff, suppliers and customers trust a firm, it needs fewer checks, contracts are simpler, and people raise problems early. Trust builds slowly through consistent conduct and is lost quickly through one visible breach.

Don't confuse vision with mission. A vision says where the organisation wants to be in the long run. A mission says what it does now, for whom and how. Nor confuse stated values with lived values: values on a wall poster count only if decisions follow them.

Where it breaks. Values that leaders do not live by breed cynicism faster than having no values at all. Values can also clash with short-term profit in a downturn, which is when they are really tested. And they are hard to measure, so they slip off the agenda.

In practice. Hire and promote people partly on values, have leaders model them, and review hard decisions against them. A commonly cited Indian example is the Tata group, where charitable trusts hold most of the shares of the parent company, Tata Sons.

For exams. Vision is at the top of a VBO's hierarchy, and trust is its core success factor.

Values set the vision; conduct earns the trust.

pairings.classic: the tasting of the king's wealth
text: Kauṭilya assumes the agency problem. Officials who handle funds will find it hard not to take some, he says, and he prescribes audits, rotation of posts and an accounts office. These are the safeguards that agency theory recommends.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.9 (conduct and embezzlement by officials)

text: The Īśa Upaniṣad opens by saying that all of this is pervaded by the divine, and advises enjoying through renunciation, without coveting anyone's wealth. Wealth is held in trust, which is the stewardship stance.
pairings.quote: ईशावास्यमिदं सर्वम् … मा गृधः कस्य स्विद्धनम् । īśāvāsyam idaṃ sarvam… mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam. Īśa Upaniṣad 1

text: Kauṭilya's line on the ruler's happiness (chapter 1) is also a governance principle: the head of the institution measures success by the welfare of those it serves.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 1.19.34

text: The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad states that truth alone prevails, and the national motto draws on it. For a VBO, trust built on consistent truthful conduct is the structural asset, and transparency in disclosure is its practice.
pairings.quote: सत्यमेव जयते नानृतम् । satyam eva jayate nānṛtam. “Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood.” Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6

text: The Saṃjñāna hymn asks for common aim, common heart and common mind, so that all may live well together. It is the language of a vision statement held by everyone in the organisation.
pairings.quote: समानी व आकूतिः समाना हृदयानि वः । samānī va ākūtiḥ samānā hṛdayāni vaḥ. Ṛgveda 10.191.4
